THE DEATH GE WINTER. • 'Pierced by the sun's bright arrows, Winter lies , With dabbled robes, upon the blurred hill-side; Fast flows the dear cold blood-' in vain he tries _T With cooling breath to cheek the flowing tide. -t!- n faintly hears-the footsteps of fair Spring • ' Advancing through the woodland to the dell. Anon she stops te hear the waters sing, Aad call the flowers that know her voice full well. Ah, now she smiles to see the glancing stream She stirs the dead leaves with her anxious feet; She stomps to plant the first awakening beam, And woos the cold Earth with wares breathings sweet, "Ali, gentle mitt,La, doth thy soul rejoice To find me thus laid low? So fair thou art! Let me but hear tho nittsic of thy voice; • Loot one bat die upon thy pitying heart. *Soon encleth life for me. Thou wilt be 'blessed; The flowering iftelds, the budding trees be thine. Grant me the pillow of thy fragrant breast; Then come, 'oblivion, I no more repine:" Thus plead the dying Winter. Site, the fair, Whose heart hath love, and only love, to give, Did -quickly lay her full warm besom hare For 'his 'cold cheek, and fondly whispered "Live:" His cold white lips close to her heart she pressed; Her sighs were mingled with each breath he drew, And when the strong life faded, on her breast Her own soft tears fell down like heavenly dew. 0 ye sweet blossoms of the whispering lea, Ye fair, frail children ef the woodland wide, 'Ye are the fruit of that dear *love which she Did give to mounded Winter ere he died. And some are tinted like her eyesof blue, Some hold the blush that on her cheek did glow, f Some from her lips have caught their scarlet hue, ;- Brit more still keep the wbiteness -of the snow. —Darns Wri2stat, he "Harper's ffar,•=ine" for Zpril.

in one to wander and pluck the sweet flowers which grew in great profusion. Soon merry little parties were scattered through the woods. Flowers were gathered for the herbarium, and the class in geology, with their teacher, wandered along the ledges of rock and collected rare specimens. At noon a horn was sounded and hungry parties came strolling in and were soon seated around the dinner, which was spread on the grass. After dinner, while the rest of the party were lounging under the trees, laugh- ing, talking and jesting, I wandered away and amused myself by following up the course of a creek, which was now almost dry, and whose steep banks were covered with ferns. I gathered a few of the rarest, when I hap- pened to spy, half way down the bank, a species unlike any I had seen, and I determined to possess it. I crept cautiously down the bank, holding on to the branches of a shrub which grew near the top. I was just reaching my hand for the coveted fern when the shrub on which I was clinging gave way, and down I went in the midst of stones and dirt. I remember catching at the bushes as I fell, and:giving one frightened shriek; then my head struck some hard substance; I tried to rise, but fell back in a dead faint. I do not know how long I lay unconscious. When I came once more to my senses ffound myself supported in the arms of Professor Richards. "You are better," he said softly, and his voice trembled. "Oh, yes, I am all. right now," and I tried to rise; but my head swam, and had not the professor. caught me I should again have fallen. I felt the dash of cool water in my face and heard some one murmur "My darling, my darling," in a voice that thrilled me tothe soul. I was naturally too strong and healthy to ;be faint long, and I was soon able to stand up and inspect my wounds. My hands were badly lacerated by the thorns which I had caught is the vain effort to save myself.;'. I had also received a severe wound on ircy temple, made by a sharp edge of a stone against which I had fallen probably. I looked at myself, bruised, drenched, and covered with mould which I had brought down in my wild career; then at the professor as he stood there hatless and agitated; and then my eyes fell on his tall silk hat still half full of water which he had brought from the neighbouring pools; then I broke into an almost hys.

"Why, Nell ,Guarnot!" I gasped, "how can you talk so? The idea of calling Prof. Richards Dickey: You certainly must be .braver than most girls to attempt a flirtation with him. I should as soon think of flying to the moon." "I am rather afraid of him now, myself:' continued Nell, "but we girt don't have muck reverenoo for any of the prefessors when out of their sight, and we have just lots of fun about Dickey. Be always wears the most immaculate of linen and the shiniest of tall hats, and he always ties his necktie just so. But I don't see why he need fix up so, when he doesn't even look at the girls." The ringing of the bell put an end to all conversation and we filed into the chapel for prayers. Professor Richards read the chapter, and as he stood there, so hand- some and dignified, I did not wonder Nell was "afraid of him."

I don't think 1 heard uuch of the hymn and prayer that followed. Somehow I had become interested in the staid, reticent professor. There was something in his tone and the glance of his eye that thrilled me. I could not help wondering what kind of a lover he would make. He would be tender, true, and constant, I was sure. The man who wasted no affection in flirtation must certainly have a wondrous store laid up for some- body. Then I wondered who that " somebody " would be. Blue eyes and golden hair she would have, because his hair and eyes were dark. But the exercises were over and we went down to recitation. Professor Richards was teacher of mathematics, and I had been in his class ever since my entrance into the school, but had thought of him only as a grave, dignified man, before whom it would not be particularly pleasant to come with poorly prepared lessons. On this day I went into the class in a state of dreamy abstraction, from which I was aroused by the Professor's voice. "Miss Larman," Nell gave me a nudge—" Don't you see the man, you may demonstrate, if you please. Class are all laughing! Professor has spoken to you three times." I arose with crimson cheeks and blundered through my demonstration making the most ridiculous mistakes, then sat down filled with mortification. The professor looked surprised but said nothing. "Your cheeks were fairly blazing," laughed Nell, as we came out into the hall. "I had a notion to call for water to put them out." "You are the most provoking girl I ever saw. I wish you'd hold your tongue, Nell Gruarnot," cried angrily,

OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDOX. THIMSDAY. Since theilleuse resumed on Tuesday, After eis mockery ,of an Easter Recess, the.debato on the second reading of the Coercion Bill .has regularly ;gone forward. Mr. Smith, after trying one or t falls with the House with the object of peremptoriky closing the debate, has found it discreet to desist, and by general consent the division, which he lately announced must betaken before Easter, will le set- tied at some early hour on Tuesday morning. The 'speaking has not been very enciting, and the ittend- nnee depressingly small. But on Monday there !IMF be expected a marked change. Mr. Gladstone islo speak on that night, an attraction which will doubtless cover the melancholy anticipation of M. W. H. Smith winding up the debate. Members who have been taking their full Easter holiday in spite of Ministerial arrangements will be baek in their places. An overwhelming attendance will respond to urgent whips on both side, and once ,again the House will bubble up with the excitement of a critical division.

What the result will be.there is zo room for doubt. The second reading will be carried by a large ma- jority, individual contributions to which will be closely scanned. It is repotted that at the last moment some halr-dosen Dissentient Liberals who voted for the first reading will abstain from further identifying themselves with the measure. The perilous slightness of the foundation upon which the position of the Government stands was indica- ted by the consternation that prevailed yesterday upon the publication of a report that Lord Harting- ton, owing to absence in Scotland, would not vets for the second reading. Lord Hartington was, when this announcement appeared, in Paris, seek- ing a little relaxation from political affairs in the genial company of Mr. Chaplin. He was imme- diately telegraphed to, and was induced to under- take to return in time for the division. But Mr. Chamberlain, happy in the accident of his visit to Skye, will not have upon his political career the fatal blot of having voted for the second reading of the Coercion Bill. This, however, is only a tempo- rary, and not very substantial advantage. Ile voted for the first reading, and cannot remain in Skye through critical divisions in committee, and on the third reading. The amazing fatuity which pursues the Govern- ment when they act apart from their Hartingtonian allies was shown in the appointment of Colonel King-Harman to an office which has been specially created for him in the Irish department. Unless it be Mr. Johnston, there is no man in the small body of Irish Conservatives whose appointment could have excited more universal condemnation. If the Government had felt the necessity of gratifying Orange feeling by appointing a Parliamentary Under-Secretary who would have been specially ir- ritating to national feeling in Ireland, there was Colonel Saunderson at hand. He is a vblent par- tisan, but he is a man of some ability and personal distinction. Colonel King-Harman does not even sit for an Irish constituency. At the General Elec- tion Ireland would not have him at any price, and he took refuge in a Kentish county district. He came

—mghter. I have told you:I was_always ridiculous. Prokessor,' I. gasped, as soon as I could speak, "you have spoiled your hat." He picked up the hat, emptied the water out of it, brushed off the dirt, and then said gravely, "You will take cold, Miss Larmaia. Shall I conduct you to the waggons ?"

finok the proffered arm, and we found a sloping place in the bank, and walked slowly back towards the others. I could not forbear glancing up in his face once or twice, but it still wore the same grave look. Tears came in my eyes. "You aro not offended with me ?" I said at last. "I know you must have saved my life, almost, but I could not help laughing." And here I broke down and cried as heartily as I had laughed. "Offended with you! I who love you so dearly, so hopelessly! Forgive me, my darling, I should not distress you thus with a love which you cannot return." He loved me, then. The blissful knowledge took away my strength, and I sank down upon a mossy log. When I had recovered myself enough to speak the professor was standing by me, entreating me in low, sad tones to "forget that he had ever spoken thus." "Don't, please," I said, as I stretched my hands toward him, "I have , loved you all the time." :-e.sialsta There—l won't tell you any more—but when we did at last rejoin the party Nell said that I looked as if to be half killed was the greatest pleasure in life." Even now, on the tenth anniversary of my wedding day, for we were married the day I graduated, I will say this much of the catastrophe—it was the most fortunate event of my life.

. GOIN' DAAN. (PH' REET 0' TRANSLATION 'S MOANED.) Ph' goin' daan as I'm tellin' yo' on isn't goin' daan i th' world, but goin* daan th' river. Na, thers a greight differunce atween these ere two things! Mooist foak as I've met wi' like goin' daan th' river wen wonct they'n tried it, but tuther sort has a bad taste i' everybudy's mouth. Riveromania is a complaint as sticks to a chap like a burr wen onct it sets in. Some as it gradely bad, but aw've naer erd o' onybody dein' on it yet, never. Nay ! aw'm th' opinion as they lookin better wen they an it. Haply it's like vaccinashun, a healthful disease, an' keeps greighter ills at arm's length. Onyway, aw've nowd som very owd men t' bi very bad on it, and yet t' a good owd age. Aw mack o' men, gentle an' simple, owd an yung, marrit or single, seem furt tack to it. Th' owd marrit uns seem furt bi more aigre abate it then th' young husbands. Haply what a yerd won on um mut- tering in his sleep as he lee at bottom ot boat, met throw a leet on th subjec'. A cud only catch a word here an' there—" bad as Mrs Caudle—quite anuf o' that—rest o' th' week—nice change—nobdy moitherin—look under th' bed—cats and dogs.' Aw this is dark to me. Aw recon it mun ha' som' meanin'. Ilaply, th' home authorities mout bi able t' explain it. So wi' them al leavit.

Aw- ve no boat a mi own, but gos daan wi them as has, as chap sed when he wur mixen in th' putty fart stop th' crack it the owd boat on th' island. They'd bin agate oth job aw winter, plesterin' an poultissin' th' poor owd invalid, an' he wur as craitchy as iver, fur it ud tack a very strong pitch plester furt draw owd age ate of other a mon ur a boat. Well, this fella, he wur mutterin' as he wur kneadin' his putty—" By jove, some folks disarve awth pleasure they getten ate o' boats! Them beggars is best off as as no boats, but gos daan wi them as has." This mon wur a filosiphur, an' didn't no it. He'd fun it ate as it wur quite possible furt pay too dear fur your whistle. "Man never is, but always to be, blest," ses th' poet, and he's reet. Sweet is antic:nation, its joys as great A. realization fully satialle.' Aw'm sure there's a greight plesser lookin' furrud to these week eend trips. Indeed, aw've yerd o' some fella as ud nought else but th' anticipation. Ile wur a cobbler, an' as sure as Monday coom rand he wur hot abate goin' daan oth' Setterday. He cud talk o' nought else. But gradjusly as Settarday geet nar he'd cool daan; an' wen Friday neet coom he'd look up to th' sky an' say it look't like rain. Hut, ses he, pointin' to th' stall, "It'll not rain here !" So he stuck to his last, an' went through th' same mogrums th' week after. Aw want furt tell yo' abate mi fost doment daan th' river in a boat. Its th' experiances of a green hand. Well, ay met th' Skipper one day, i' War- rington, an' he axt mi would a like a trip daan th' river a Setterclay. Aw sed aw thought aw shud. "Well," ses he, "be at Atherton's Quay at one o'clock ; ' an' a was, fur a think it such a rung thing furt break a promise like this. My conscience is clear abate this, fur a never do disapint a mon as axes mi furt pleas mi sen. Fruits o' bein' gradely brought up, yo sin. So aw wur theer to th' minite. But aw wur not bi misel though; there wur men wi basldts, an' sum wi bundle ankichers wi corners o' loaves stickin' out on um, an' sum wi' big stone bottles ther honds—these wer waitre men, ars is a teetotal boat—aw intent on charitable deeds—feedin' th' hungry an' haply nainistrire to th' sick. Som' o' are crew had wat thi cawd pill boxes full.e kitchen fisic. While t' tide wur runnin' up they wur agate a stowin' away aw these cumberments. Aw notist won on em, Tommy Bobbington, he wur varry pertick- ler abeawt wheere he put anowd two pand meat tin three-parts full o' gress jow worms, as heed brought wi' him i' a bass-mat alung wi' his grub. Tuther chaps wur chaffin' an' axiia' wur he gooin' t' feed um again ? an' tellin' him furt put his snig-beef wheere it wouldn't get upset or weet afore its time. But they aw agreed in sayin' "If they'll poo at one eend, aw will poo at t'other." Na this is one o' thoose dark sayin's as needs interpretin—it means o' this anon, as th' penny numbers say—an' .Bt3 they very often remark— (To be continued in our next.)

RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. GOOIN' TO TIP FAIR! Heigh, Nan! Does this jackut fit weel ? Is t' fither o reet mi hat? Just tek thoose odd things—put 'em by— Be keerful! dorn't deet mi best brat! Aw want to torn eawt gradely nice— What's up? dosta say; neaw dorn'd stare, Brush me deawn, an' aw'll bring summat back— Aw'm going wi' Bobby to th' fair! It's four o'clock neaw! He'll be /on Waitin' for mo, at th' loyne end, bi th' gate; He's a playn, daycent lad, an' aw weren'd Let him stan' long thro' me bein' late. Mi ears they're fair itchin' to hear Luv's music so' soft fro' his tung ! This hat doesn't fit reet at th' back; Put id gradely, id wern't t,ek thee lung! Five minutes past four! Aw'll be off! Arta sure as ther's nowt eawt o' place? Wey, ther's summat ut's smutted mi cheek. Reych th' flannel! aw'll just wipe mi face; Iffi neck's rayther bare, if this glass Con be trusted; hey, heaw time does fly! Come, Nan, side thoose oddments away— Wheereyer th' world is mi tie? Its getten ten minutes past neaw, At havof past aw sed awd be theer ; Mi hanketcher's theer uppo th' Reych up for% an' chuck id mo here! Aw wonder wod Bobby ull say When he sees me donned up like this? Aw know, if ther's nobry i'th' loyne, He'll gie mo a hearty good kiss! Come Nan, find mi gowd brooch, be sharp, Aw hey'nd a minute to loyse ! Nay, dornd thee look black, cause awm cram'd,— Aw kornd help fro' mekkin' a noyse, It's a quarter past neaw, yarra near, A lass is quare tempert as loves ! Aws' hey to run welly o th' way— Stop Nan! wheer ta puttin' mi gloves? Aw dornd like this fleawnee baggin' eawt, Here, pin id up tightish at th' back, That's id,—its a lot better neaw,— Awst hey to den l 6ff in a crack! Ged th' scithors an' just clip thad braid Ut's jaggin' on th' edge o' mi skirt. Hey dear, heaw thad clock rambles on— Wod a flutter ther is i' mi heart! 'Find mi poss ! Its i' one o' them..drawers ! Confeawnd id—neaw con id be? Just look on to th' cornish.—Nowt timer? It's happen th' cubbort !—just see! Un mi new umbrella's upstairs— Mi heyd's like a shippon beawt thatch! Aw'mamythert. It's torned hawf-past neaw— Dosta know wheer eawr Turn put mi watch ?

• • • • • • Well if ever aw see sitch a do ! Aw've come to mi senses at last. Thad clock's a feaw-faced fawse owd foo ! Hawf an heawr un ten minutes too fast! Aw'll sit me deawn neaw for a bit, For mi heart plays a easier tune, An awm nod beawn to let Bobby see As aw'm anxious, thro gooin too soon. Wod dosta expect when aw come? Aw'll bring thee a fairin' as suits ; Summat useful an' nice,—Nan, reych thr brush, Aw'll just tek this dust off mi boots. Aw believe Bobby's beawn to buy t' ring ! Wheer's th' comb P—aw've just ruffled mi hair Good day, Nan. He's yon !—Bless his heart! Aw'm gooin wi' Bobby to th' fair! Jecz o' Ames.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF COMMONS—Turs.

TEE SPEAKER RETURNS THANKS.—The SPEAKER, ap• parent tT much improved in health, resumed his place in the chair shortly before four o'clock. In doing so, he said: I have to acknowledge the indulgence of the House, shown to me last week, during my indisposition. I also desire to express my obligstions to the Chairman of Ways and Means for occupying my chair during my absence, Tear, hear.) QUESTIONS. - -

In answer to a question from Dr. Wallace, Mr. W. H. S'lars said the Board of Inland Revenue were empowered by law to accept compromise fines when it thought proper in mitigation of penalties incurred by persons selling excisable liquors on qther than licensed premises, or for other offences against the excise laws. In reply to Sir Savile Crossley, Baron de WORMS said the Board of Trade would communicate with the Foreign Office, with the view of transmitting officially to the Belgian Government a copy of the report of the Com- mittee on the complaints of damage inflicted on British drift-net fisheries in the North Sea. The Board of Trade hoped thp Belgian .Vrovernrnent would see fit to co- operate with her Majesty's Government, in order to give effect to the suggestion contained in the report. Mr. ROBERTSON asked would the Government, before the close of the second reading debate on the Crimes Bill, lay on the table a statement of the names of resident magistrates in Ireland, the date of the appointment of each, and his previous occupation, if any. (Hear, hear.) --Mr. BALFOUR said a return giving these and other details was in preparation, and would be laid on the table as soon as ready.

div.head: CRIMES BILL DEBATE.
div.p: THE CRIMES BILL DEBATE.

The debate on Sir Bernard Samuelson's amendment to the second reading of the Criminal Law Amendment (Ireland) Bill was resumed.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND rose amid Ministerial cheers in a somewhat thin Heim. He asked the House to bestow a fair and candid consideration on the provisions of the Govern- ment bill, and see how far they justified the language which had been applied to the measure by its opponents. Speaking as to the condition of Ireland, he referred to the charges of several judges, as already quoted, in justification of the acticn taken by the Government, and indignantly denied on their behalf that either of them could be accused of ever having allowed their politics to bias their performance of duty. Indeed he challenged the hon, members opposite to prove their charges of impropriety, and at this point was met by the exclamation from Mr. M. J. Kenny: The House won'tallow us to do so. In continuation the Attorney- General for Ireland went at some length into the class of cases heard before the jUdges at the different assizes, and dwelt upon the largelproportion of crime which bore a political or a,E.Trarian complexion. He also called attention to the number of cases in which crime was not detected, or in which it was found impossible to obtain evidence on which to obtain convictions when evidence was obtainable. Speaking of the proposed change of venue, he said it was admitted that trial by jury had in many parts of Ireland al;solutely broken down, and, this being so, he would regard nothing as more absurd than to say that crinie should go un- punished rather than that effectual means shotild be taken for securing the du a administration of the law. He hoped, however, in regard to this provision that it would not be necessary to have frequent recourse to it. (Ironical cheers from the Opposition.) With regard to that portion of the bill which dealt with summary jurisdiction, he pointed out that this was not the first time provision had been made for dealing with offenders by summary process. The fact was that hardly a session ever paSsed that did not witness the passing of some measure for amending, or ri alteng, in one way or another. Suinmary jurisdiction conferred on magistrates and other legal functionaries, in one or other of the three kingdoms. He denied that the resident magistrates in Ireland were any more executive officers than the. justices of the peacti, and stated that every possible •safeguard had been inserted in the bill, by way of appeal and otherwise, to ensure that the powers it conferred should be fairly ad- ministered. With regai'd to, the boycotting prqvisions, he contended that they were of a• mild and reasonable character, and as to the powers.of proclamation he jus- tified that portion of the. measure as necessary to the enforcement of the law. • He also defended the proposal to make the measure a perpetual one, remarking that the great fault of previous repressive Acts had been that they were only passed for limited periods. . _ _ _ . .

_ Mr. CHILDERS, who rose amidst loud Opposition Cheers, said in opposing the bill hehaci several admissions to make. In his opinion some of the provisions of the bill would not be objectionable if they were made part of the general law of the country., He agreed with many who had said there was much in the state of Ireland in connection with rents timi so forth that ought to be de- plored, but, at the same time, much of this was due to the rejection last autumn by the present Government of the bill brought in Ipy M. Parnell. '(Hear, hear.) He further admitted that there had been in Ireland an in- crease in the amount of crime during the past year, but he contended that the Government had totally failed to show that that slight increase formed any real justification for such a measure as the present. He would aLso admit that, as having ;sup- ported Coercion Bills promoted by fcirmer governments, he might be open to the charge of inconsistencies in the course he was now taking, but he denied that any occu- pant of the Treasury bench, except the Chancellor of the Exchequer, could throw that charge in hi a face without inconsistency on his own part. (Opposition cheers.) It was, he believed, a fact that no fewer than BO members sitting on the Conservative side of the House had before the Last election declared against any further measure of Coercion for Ireland, while the Prime Minister himself had stated it to be impracticable and impossible to reimpose upon Ireland a measure like the Crimes Act. Mr. Childers went on to object to the bill on three main grounds—First, that it was strongly opposed by the representatives of five-sixths of the Irish people; secondly, that there was no such in- crease of crime in Ireland, as to justify the introduction of the present bill; and, thirdly, that it was proposed for the first time in the history of such measures th make permanent the intended alteration of the Irish 6riminal law. The right hon, gentleman complained that it was proposed to use the permanent powers of the bill only within certain limited districts, ,and to confer, their administration, so far as summary jurisdiction went, upon the resident magistrates, whom he held to be unfit by previous training to exercise them, especially in rases involving the application of the extreme provi- sions of the Whiteboy Acts, and the legal construction of-t Ate word "-conspiracy." He strongly 'cond'emnedthe proposal to try Iris la prisonep in England as one of the worst provisions of the meashre, and, putting the ques- tion from a contrary point of view, asked what would have bee said if it had ever been proposed to send Eng- listunen2for trial out of their own conntry. (Opposition cheers.) He also protested against the power sought to be given to the Executive in cases of dangerous associa- tions, and ridiculed the looseness of the'definition given by the bill of what a dangerous association was' to be, namely, an organisation calculated to put any person in fear of a loss of business, an accusation which, he said, was applicable to the Primrose 'League in this country, as well as to every railway company as against the in- terests of stage coach proprietor& In conclusion the right hon. gentleman expressed a preference for a well- considered plan of Home Ride, tinder which Ireland could govern herself in matters of purely domestic busi- heas, to the alternate doses of coercion 'area flattery which had hitherto been applied to that cowl*.

_ Mr. Sniw-Srxwarcr spoke in support of the bill, as , necessitated by the inability of the Executive to cope with the crime that was being corrnnitted in Ireland. , _ Mr. Mtrx.iin FERGtrSON, in opposing the bill, denied that any case had been made out fir such a measure, and re- marked that were it proposed to apply such a bill to Scotland the effect of such an announcenient would be to produce a very considerable stir in that country. The hon. gentleman argued that it was by conferring upon Ireland free institutiottl that they must hope for the real settlement of the Irish question. • Mr. W. C. flarrun supported the bill, as called for by the state of things in Ireland, and especially by the , action of the supporters of the National League, and the promoters of the plan of carepaign. Mr. J. STuarrr characterisedas a delusion the idea that - discontent was the work of agitation in Ireland,.as urged on the Government side of the House, and contended that agitation was in reality the result of discontent. Mr. J. E. REDMOND (NVexford), who opposed the bill, pointed out that for the first time in the 'history of Irish Coercion Bills it was now proposed to discard. the funda- mental principle on which hitherto these exceptional measures had been proposed, in order to meet excepo tional emergencies..-Moreover with regard to the offence of boycotting, which the bill' wa.s said to have been mainly designed to suppress, there are at the present tune fewer cases than were known to exist at the ' tune Lord Salisbury in 1885 decided On doing without the renewal of the Crimes Act. The Sabra SzenzrAnv, speaking on behalf of the Government, repeated the admission that had been pre- viously made by his colleagues that, the present bill was not based on an excessive and bnormal amount of crime in Ireland, although, he said, this argument should not be pressed too far by the Opposition,. inasmuch as statistics now in the hands of the Govern- ment showed that since last October agzr4an crime huh incieaSecl .85 per cent. This, he held, was attributed to the effect of organisations and combinations throughout the country, and the outrages were, he cow:fir:dad, quite nurnerottS, enough to warrant the prtisent action of the Government. (Ministerial cheers.) That trial by jury had broken down was admitted, and even the con- stant resort of the Crown officials M the right of chal- lenge—or what was termed"jury-packing" on the other side of the House-Odious as such a system must be to those-who had to adopt it, was in itself a proof' of the necessity of this measure. The bill did not create new offences, it merely tnnk those which were known-to the law, and., by making them the subject of summary jurls. diction.-relleved Irish juries of a series of trials for which they-were acknowledged, to be unfitted, further- more, the measure did rzotstnle-at lawful combinations ; it woe aimed' emir a.t. conspiracies of a well-know character, and Elid not.. includet,setlitidn, or-treason; or other-o.ffenceeof the most serious class. Thp-offances dealt-with by ill-the b 'were such as wOuld-i3e- 'best, dealt , within a enramarrfashion—offences emallinthemselves.

A MEDICAL sTuDENvs r.rurri4N. At Warrington County ijourt, o Thursdayibefore his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, a case was heard in which George C. Gilroy, headmaster of the Winwlck Grammar School, sued Herbert Thompson, medical student, Larkfield, Earlestown, on a claim for £3 3s for tuition. Mr. H. J. Longton (Warrington), .who appeared for the plaintiff, said that the claim ,was for services rendered in conne3tion with the, preliminary examination for the medical profession. Defendant had an interview in March of last year with the plaintiff, who told him that his terms for tuition, were three guineas per quarter during the time of study, and three guineas when the candi- date had passed his examination. The terms were accepted. and Mr. Thompson paid in advance. In July last, year, shortly after be became 21, he went in for the exarnipation and failed. Study with the plaintiff was resumed, and in October last defendant passed his examination. The money sued for was the three guineas stipulated for on his passing. Mr: Longton added that he Understood that a plea of in- fancy had been set up, but he did not think that would hold good, as it had been laid down that an infant might bind himself to pay for his good teaching, whereby he might profit himself afterwards. Then, again, the defend ant resumed his duties after be had attained his majority. Mr. Hodgkinsen (Bolton) who appeared for the defence, said the agreement was simply for three guineas' a quarter. When defendant first saw Mr. Gilroy something was said about a bonus as lee was leaving the house, but no asnount was mentioned and no agreement made as to that. He did not see how this could come under the head of a claim for necessary instruction, for the fees for the tui- tion had been regularly. paid. His •Honour, after hearing evidence, referred to,a letter handed in, written by defen- dant to plaintiff, in which be repudiated his liability, to pay a bonus, saving that as he was not successful at the first examination his liability ceased. The letter also added that he could not afford to pay at present,. but might some day later. His Honour remarked that that letter left the impression that defendant knew a bonus had been sti- pulated for. With regard to the plea of infancy the defen- dant's third quarter of tuition began after he came of age, and therefore he should think the contract, being thus renewed, was binding. He gave judgment for the plaintiff, payment to be made in a month.
A severe snowstorm visited North Essex on Thursday morning, and the fall.was blinding. The snow lay three inches deep, and the cold was intense.

( but of a nature that made their constant perpetration a source of irritation and annoyance to the community. Summary jurisdiction had, it should be remembered, been largely extended in England of late years. As to the graver cases of murder, arson, and so4forth, if the Government-were right that juries in-Ireland could not be entrusted -with the trial of the fighter-cases, surely they were equally right in the proposal they rnacleas to the ' trial of • the more serious ones, especially after the refusal of the Irish judges on a former occasion to undertake such trials unaided by juries. Let the House amend the clause if they pleased, and give the alternative of a trial by Irish judges or an English jury, and he believed that in cpubt cases the accused persons would select •hi English tribunal. rhesewere the broad outlines Qn which.alone he-intended to touch. He denied that this measure was as severe as the Act of 1270-orthe Crimes Bill of 1882, both of which gave the Crown Executive far more arbitrary powers than were asked for inthis bill, which he did not hesitate to say was the mildest measure that had been proposed for Ireland during the list 17 years. Mr. STANSFELD, who was cheered by the Opposition. .ftemsed the Home Secretary of having at the com- mencement of his speech given up his whole ease by admitting that: he had none that was founded on statistics_ The Government, he argued, were condemned by the report of their own Coti:- mission and the bill they had brought it would intensify and aggravate the state of things against which it was aimed, rather than provide a sufficient remedy. The right 11013. gentleman severely con- demned the proposal to place in the hands of resident magistrates the summary decision of cases of conspiracy and so forth, and contended theta Govern- ment which could not do without the *suspension of trial by jury was not a fit Government for Ireland. It was, he maintained, inconsistent to coerce the Irish people, and allow them to retain their representa- tion in that House. This question he held to be a people's question, and it would be for the people at the next eler.tion to- decide it. He and those with whom he acted believed that the 'verdict of the people when taken upon this question would be against coercion, and in favour of a system of self-government for the Irish people. • The House adjourned at 12-40 a.m.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDWESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at twenty-five minutes past , twelve.

THE COERCION BILL. The debate on Sir Bernhard Sarnuelson's amendment to the second reading of the Criminal Law Amendment !Ire- land) Bill wassesurned by Lord H. BRUCE, who argued that the bill, though it would affect no one who obeyed the law, would protect innocent and well-disposed people.—Sir W. FOSTER warmly supported the conciliatory policy of Mr. Gladstone, and thought from the conduct of the landed aristocracy and the clergy that a bill of the kind introduced by the Government was as much needed for England as for Ireland.—Sir HENRY HOLLAND believed the people were strongly convinced of the impolicy of establishing a hostile parliament in Ireland, and said if the Government found that the feeling of the country was against them they would cheerfully retire from office. The Government were ready if necessary to test the real feeling of the country by a general election, but the question had been put fairly be- fore the country at the last election, and the country decided against Home Rule. Mr. GULLY asserted that the bill was impolitic, ill-timed, ard unnecessary. The SOLICITOR • GENERAL for SCOTLAND denied that the measure would in any way . interfere with the liberty of the subiect, as after the passing 4of the bill every Irishmen would be able to do everything which was legal to an Englishman or Scotchman.—Sir U. Key-Salarrrarevonra expressed his own 'strong feeling, which he said was shared by his constituents, that we could ill afford to add one more to the long tale of mistakes this country had committed in its dealings with Ireland. The bill was doing much to clear the vision of Liberals through-. out the country. He objected to the proposed change of venue te England because it was repugnant to English feel- ing, contrary to constitutional practice, and, above all, was a proposal the most insulting to Ireland that could possibly have been brought forward. As regarded crime there was no case for the bill, and the whole case for it rested on agrarian discontent, which arose from the land system, absentee pro- prietors, high rents, and evictions.—On the motion of Mr. BAGGALLAY the debate was adjourned. Birsonrroorsors.—Mr. KENNY having moved the second reading of the SolicitOrs's Annual Certificate Duty Bill, Mr. TOKIJNSON talked it out.—The Coal Mines, itc., Regulation Bill was read a second time,Ahe Committee being appointed for 2nd May.—Colonel KING-HARMAN moved for leave to bring in a bill ta amend the law relating to the office of as- sistant inspector general and of county inspector and dis- trict inspector in Ike Royal Irish Constabulary.—Mr. BIGGA.R objected, and the motion was consequently post- poned. The MUSS adiourned at ten minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIIMSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'elock. • THE 'UNDER-SECRETARY FOR IRELAND—SeveraI awk- ward questions were put in connection with Colonel King- Harman's recent appointment.—Mr. Jolts MORLEY wished to know by what authority the office of Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Ireland was constituted; the conditions under which it was held, and whether it was proposed to attach any salary to the office.—Mr. BALroun replied that there was DO salary attached to the office, and that the Government • had taken pains .to as- certain that their action was legal. Mr. GLAD- STONE inquired if the seat was vacated, and upon being told that it was not as it was not an office of profit under the Crown. the right hon. gentleman remarked that he once had the honour to serve sincier a Conservative Gov- ernment as Commissioner to the lonian Islands, and under the advice of the law officers of the Government, although be received no sklary, his seat for Oxford University was vacated, and he was re-elected. Some of the Irish members wished to know whether the Colonel watt a member of Orange and other secret societies. and whether be was not at one time secretary to the Home Rule League in Dublin, but replies were not given to these questions. THE BUDGET—Mr. SMITH informed hon. members that he had no intention of proposing an adjournment for a short holiday next week, and said Ile hoped the Budget would be taken on Thursday. THE COERCION BILL.—Thc debate on the amendment to the motion for the second reading of the Crimes Bill was resumed by Mr. BUM-ALLAY, who declared that it was the duty of the Government to press the measure forward, and when passed to put it in force.—Sir L. PLAYFAIE, argued that tbere was nothing in the condition of crime in Ireland to justify apll which the Government dared not apply to Great Britain. The pith of the bill rested on the clauses dealing with associations tainted with crime, which gave a political officer—the • Lord Lieutenant—power to declare what was crime and whether an associa- tion was a dangerous one or not. Mr. RITCHIE said he was convinced that the only policy which the country would approve was one of firmness and determina- tion in asserting the supremacy of law and order in Ireland. —Mr. AMBROSE thought it a great merit of the bill that the Government intended to deal with a particular class a minor offences by summary proceeding.—Sir J.. GOLDSMID complained of the atteiopta Made to coerce Liberal Unionists by threats, and condemned the speech of Mr. Burns at Bat- tersea, on Batordaq.—Mr. WHITBREAD, continuing the• debate, &indented the Government bill.—Mr..Porrest Ful- ton and Mr. Itenny havieg spoken, the debatewas adjourned oat the motion f of Sir W. HARCOURT. ' • SUPREME COURT OF JUDICATURE (IRELAND) BILL, &C.— Tile Bill pasted through cemmittee without aniend moo, and by leave the House was read a third' time.--The Hyde Park Corner New Streets) Bill was read a third time.-- Colonel King-Harnian brought in a ' bill to amend tbe law relating to the Royal Irish Constabelary, which was read a first time. The House adjourned at twenty minutes to two.

The lambing season in Westmoreland has been an un- usually successful one. Most of the ewes have a couple, and three and even four lambs tip no exception.
On Monday-night two young men wereinapleasure boat together off Tynemouth, when one of them, William Walls,_in.a.ttemptin,g to change seats, fell overboard and was drowned.
A fire occm-red onMonday in a private house in Quebec- street, near the Marble . Arch, London. An aged lady, named Ellen Jellicoc, was dreadfully injured, and she died shortly afterwards.'

Ccurns.idArroir nr A CarrAos.—The Bishop of Lich- field, on attending a confirmation service at Wolver- hampton a few' days ago was informed that a little girl, who had intended being present at the service, lay seri- ously El at home. His lordship, unsolicited, proceeded to the girl's borne, that of a working man, and having robed in the'lritchen performed the service at the bed- side of the invalid. Tire ICAPUNDA DISASTEIL—WiIIiam Milikin, late master of the Ada Mehnore, which, as will be remembesed, was the vessel which came into collision with the emigrant ship Kapunda, was, on Saturday, in London, charged at the Bow-street Polite-court, with having neglected to carry lights on his vessel as required by the Act. It was stated %hat for a considerable 'number of consecutive nights after rounding Cape Ildrn no lights whatever were carried. The defendant pleaded guilty:, and was fined £5O, out of which £lO costs was deducted. A prison warder, attended by Swansea policemen, on Sunday discovered hidden in a hedge the greater part of £333 which was stolen recently from a coachman., who three months ago drew it from the bank for his master, Mr. Player, of Clydach. A man named Huictable was found guilty of the robbery, and last week he was sent into penal servitude for five years. The prison warder heard HuAtable tell his wife were the money was. She informed the police, but they failed to find it. The warder then joined in the search ; hence the discovery.

• A FATAL CARMISIL-At the Stafford Borough Police Court on Monday, three men, named Arthur Findon „George Clayton, and Martin Carney, were charged with felony. On Saturday night a jar containing. two gallons of ,whisky was stolen, presumably by the prisoners, from the Sun Inn, Stafford, and early on Sunday morning the police were called to a lodging-house in the town where Thomas Durham, son .of the keeper of the house, lied died during the night. The stolen jar was found in thehouse, empty. Durham is believed to have died from alcoholic poisoning. Clayton was reductid to a helpless state, and had to she treated at the Infirmary. The prisoners were remanded pending the inquest. ,

SHIPPING DISASTERS -On Saturday the large sailing vessel Prince Victor, from New York to Sharpness, with 10,000 barrels of paraffin, got aground near Beachy. The tide rushed into the cabin and drowned the captain's wife and child. The vessel was got off, but was again blown ashore at Woolaston, where she is now lying.—A collision occurred on Saturday afternoon, near the mouth of the Gironde, between the English steamer Durley, from Fiume, and the Dutch 'steamer Sirius, bound for Amsterdam. The former sank. The creW of the Burley were saved by the Cutter of the pilot who was in charge of the vessel, and were transferred to an English steamer whibh was entering the river., The Sirius 'sustained serious damage, and will have to put back to Bordea-ux for repairs.

ME GOOD TEMPLA:RBr*-The eighteenth annual session of the Grand Lodge of England of the Independent Order of Good Templars was opened on Monday at the Memorial Hall, Farringdon-street, London; Mr. Joseph Malins, worthy chief templar, presiding. Six hundred and seven members of the Grand Lodge were present, in addition to 297 qualified applicants for grand Lodge member- ship, who were afterwards admitted. The reports showed a membership of 66,268, in 1,686 lodges. Various committees were appointed, and deputations from kindred societies were welcomed.—ln the evening a public reception was held in the City Temple Dr. Richardson presiding. On the motion of the Rev. Temple, Barker, prebendary of St. Paul's, seconded by the lion. Conrad Dillon a resolution was passed cordially welcom- ing the Grand Lodge and recognising the order as a mighty instrument for uplifting humanity.—Mr. Malins acknowledged the resolution.—Mrs. Lucas, Rev. G. Glad- stone, and other speakers followed.

• MURDERS IXPIANCE.—Cases of the most cynical and cold-blooded murders continue to be reported from the French provinqes. •A lad 17 years of age, named Espen- ette, has just been arrested for the murder of an old woman named Guillermet, at Mably, near Roanne. The woman was found drowned in a well last month, and there Was no clue to how she came there until Espenette's mother denounced her Son. On being questioned he frankly admitted having stolen Madame GuiDermet's money, and having drowned her to *fent her from in- forming against him. He Male behind her as she was drawing water, and pushed her into the well. As she grasped the rope to which the bucket was attached and kept herself above the water he threw down on her head a water-can, an iron pot, and a small barrel, and finally succeeded in his hideous, crime. He gave all these details with the greatest indifference. At Ferfa.y, near ThSthune. a woman: named Roselle Dufour has been found mur- dered, her head being completely severed from the body. As usual, the object or the murder was plunder. •

A REIUMSABLE VOTAGE.—Particulars are published of an interview with three adventurous mariners who have just succeeded in voyaging from Natal to Dover in a cockle-shell of a boat, twenty feet long by four feet six inches beam, and drawing four and a half feet of water. Not only did the three men navigate the boat through the tempestuous waste of waters, but she was constructed by their own hands. The captain, named Nilson, had tempOrarily given tip' the sea, and had a store and blacksmith's shop in the Orange Free State, being assisted by his brother and a man named Olsen, a forgeman by trade. Business being dull, they resolved upon making the adventure, naming ' their vessel the Homeward Bound after she was built. The difficulties of their voyage may be apprehended to some -extent from the fact that it occupied ten months. Their .achieve- merit is a magnificent testimohy to their pluck and en• durance, and it can only be regretted that such qualities have not found some more useful outlet than the making of a totally unnecessary voyage.

Sw'RRI bi,yOnets and 150,000 leather iaibbaisls: Thor-pattern required is 1887 Thirty thousand are required for Oelivery by the 31st A 'rch, 1888, and the remainder to. be spread over two or three years, at the discretion of the Secretary for War. Up to this time Sheffield manufacturers have complained that the War Office hive changed the pat- tern so frequently that the worlevlas not worth their attention, but the unusually heavy, requirements now estimated may lead to Sheffield enteritig vigorously into compeOfion with Tolifigen, the seat of the German manu- facture. The application for tenders became publicly known on Monday. At present Sheffield supplies the steel for swords raa,de.at Ilirminglaam—The Government also invite tenders for a large quantity of cartridges and fuse, as well as 30,000 common shells, 12,500 steel shells, and 7,500 case shot.' Three Sheffield firms are now engaged on orders, for steel proiectfies for tpse overnwent,: One firtirecliiras to have discovered e steel shell sup4ior to anything yet produced by. the French manufacturers.

PotERTY Arm Scicrne : A HisinEsslgo SI‘ORT.—A suicide Of a most distressing character occurred in Leeds on 'Monday. About seven a.m. the landlady of the Beech Hotel, Wortley, noticed the three young children of her next door neighbour, Mrs. Harriet Turner. stand- ing crying bitterly outside the house. When interro- gated, • they stated that their mother was hangik up dead, and on. investigation this VbaS fond to bb the case. The poor woman had suspended herself from a nail in the wooden ceiling by means of a towel andsome tape, and when cut down was fond to be quite dead. For several weeks past she had been in a low state, owing to her poverty. Three years ago her husband deserted her; and is now believed to lie living in Glasgow with another woman. ' The deceased, who was 30 years of age and respectably connected, has been supported by her_brother, who is an hotel keeper in Stockton, but latterly he has sent the usual weekly allowance (55.) to the deceased's eldest child, a girl of 16, who is in service •in Leeds, and she has paid the rent With it. The deceased was frequentlY urged to go to the workhouse, but she always used Nearly every article of furniture and 'dress had been paWned or sold, and the house was quite 'bare with the exception of two tables, two chairs, and a box. In the cupboard were found a few dry crusts, some of which, the children said, their mother had. soaked in water for their breakfast that morning. A Sri/axon CAREED: ELOPEMENT AND MURDER.— A woman named Victor, with a pronounced suicidal' mania, has just been condemned (says a Paris telegram) to six months' imprisonment for having caused- the death of her little Child during one of her attempts at self- destruction. She •laid herself, with her infant, on her bed, after lighting a pan of charcoal, but after a time a neighbour burst open the door. The child was already dead, but the woman's life was saved. Hers is a very sad story. Madame Victor had for some years after her marriage led an exemplary life. liar huaband was a steady'workman ; but for some unaccountablereason the woman suddenly fell madly in love with a bootmaker named Cordier, and after some time, aashe could not live withhim,she persuaded him to die withher. Accordingly, one day when the husband was out, the couple kindled charcoal in her bedroom, but as'it had no effect on them Cordier suggested that they should try to stifle themselves in a smaller chamber. Again there -was no result„ so they placed a noose round their neckstand pulled it with all their might But Cordier and his.mis- tress seem to have had the nine lives of the proverbial cat; so, after trying to strangle and suffocate themselves with a zeal and an energy worthy of a better cause, the man proposed that they should solve the problem by eloping. Madame Vittor consented, and off they went with her little,child. But after a week Cordier's flame-died.ont, and he left his mistress in the lurch. Thewoman,seeing no issue out of her difficulty, again bad recourse-to the charcoal-p-, which proved fatal to her infant, but not to herself. She-was taken to the hospital, where she so ofbm. endeavoured to make away with herself that she had in be placed in a strait-watitcoat,Whiloberhusbatid was sent fortcrease her mind bygiving her-a full,par- don. The poor man, who-has smce.bzukenJiis.leg, new lies in a precarious state hrthe same hospital.

• A farmer named Ahearne has been arrested at Dun- garvan' charged with setting fire to the house of an evicted tenant, and also to his own house. He admitted the crime, but added that he was forced by armed moon- lighters to do it Three moonlighters were committed for trial on Satur- day from Listowel, charged with entering the house of a man named Brosniham, of Knockbrack. The principal Crown witness has left the country, and a warrant has been issued for his apprehension. The Lord-Lieutenant and Privy Council of Ireland, under the Peace Preservation Act, have again made a proclamation at Limerick and tho parts snore imme- diately affected, of the Act relating to the importation ,of arms and ammunition into Ireland. The prociama- tion is looked upon as significant, in view of the Crimes Bill passing into law. - -

At an early hour on Saturday, a fire broke out in the extensive mineral water manufactory of Messrs. Cantrell and Cochrane, Belfast, and although the brigade arrived in a few minutes from the station close by, almost the entire concern was destroyed. The stores at the rear of the premises were saved, but the damage amounts to many thousands of pounds. An attempt was made on Saturday to evict a farmer named Daniel Grace from his holding near Dunmanway, West Cork. The tenant and his wife held the constabu- lary and bailiffs at bay by throwing stones from the upper story. Having cut away the staircase, a fusilade was poured by Grace and his wife, the latter holding an infant in her left arm, while she used her right for hurl- • ing the missiles. • The bailiffs and police got into the lower portion of the house, and cut through the floor, which they attempted to pull down with ropes. For eight hours the resistance was maintained, and the attempted eviction had to he abandoned at sunset, ' - - -r On Sunday there" ni6itei noting in Belfast, ma the Orange Shankhill-road. This on the face of it would seem to account for nearly twopence of the fourpenny increase; but on turning to the Report, we find that the total estimate in the. Sanitary department for the coming year is positively less than the estimate for the year previous—namely £8,739 9s. for the coming year as compared with £9,082 is. for the twelve months just expired. That there may be no misapprehension, we may add that, in answer to a question put by the Mayor, Alder- man BURGESS, as Chairman of the Sanitary Committee, said the estimate of £8.739 9s included the £r,ooo to come out of the rates to cover the excess in expenditure on Long- ford works. If this be so, it follows that if the Council had not been called upon to pay the extra £r,ooo this year, the estimate of the Sanitary Committee, instead of being, as it is even now, £3.4.3 less than the total of the previous year, would have been reduced by £1,343. This would have permitted, so far as this department is concerned, of a reduc- tion in the rates of z/d in the pound. But as the 21,000 is to be paid at once, and, as that is, roundly speaking, equivalent to twopence in the pound, the Sanitary Committee stand before the public with a reduction in their estimate equal to a halfpenny in the pound. The explanation of the increase of fourpence in the pound is not to be found there; and we are still at a loss to know where it is to be found. It may be that the retepayers are suffering througn having to pay interest or money which is as yet lying idle thro,..- gn the Bridge-street improvement lout if this be so, why was it not me7..4loll'ed at the Council meeting? There 19 obvious need for further inquiry; and wo trust that further questions will be put at the next meeting so that the in- habitants may know why they are being called upon to meet a considerable increase in rates which are, to begin with, notoriously high.

THE Easter Holiday has passed over very pleasantly; the weather has been dry and bright; vast numbers of people have had a change of air and of scene; and there has been no serious railway accident to mar the recollection of a season of enjoyment. We are having a late spring; the buds have been holding themselves in readiness to come forth gaily dressed ; but they have shrunk under the sharp east wind and night frosts ; and thus it is that, though we are in the middle of April, the trees are leafless. It is a case in which, as Coleridge says in " Christabel," "the spring comes slowly up this way," but still it does come: and if we have not reached the period when it "unlocks the flowers to paint the laughing soil," we all see and feel some of the signs of the ever•new miracle of the year. Does not Tennyson tell us that— In the Spring a fuller crimson comes upon the robin's breast; In the Spring the wanton lapwing gets himself
another crest; In the Spring a livelier iris changes on the burnished

c, dove; In the Spring a young man's fancy lightly turns to thoughts of love. It is theretore in every way fitting, assuming that the weather is tolerable. that our work- ing population should make holiday at Eastertide. The young do not, to be sure, trouble much about the weather; for Corin does not concern himself to observe whether the wind is east, or east by north-east, when he _ _

—sports with Amarillis in the shade Or with the tangles of Necera's hair. Still if it be wet, downright wet, it damps one's spirits as well as clothing; and Corin had .better defer "popping the question, if he finds that the rain has spoiled the feather in Newra's hat. No damsel with a proper regard for the fitness of things could be ex- pected to whisper " Yes " under such de- pressing circumstances. The older birds, who have paired and nested years ago. I usually feel something of the spirit of the old time come over them when spring is here. Easter is the first break after what may have, been a lone and hard winter; and the relaxa- tion it affords is hailed as a momentary re- 1 lief from the constant pressure of" carking cares." It is true that it costs something to get to the seaside, or to visit distant relations and friends—for the ordinary folk that live now-a-days, cannot, witch - fashion, cross the country on a broomstick; and there are some men deeply learned in statis- tics who will calculate to a nicety how much is lost to the nation throuah " hands" and " works " ' being idle for a whole day at Easter. The figures, when they stare at you in a row, are really appalling ; but these wise men never give us the total of the gain to health, and life, and good feeling which comes of a happy holiday. Man does not live by bread alone, and there is some- thing better to look at, once in a while, than the mine, the factory, or the furnace. Mother-earth, old as she is, is ever young, and when she is bright and glad with the glory of spring, her children should make themselves bright and glad, too, with a holi- day so well spent that it shall be remembered as a holy day.

Gradually but surely a strong current of feeling is rising throughont the country against the Coercion policy of the Govern- ment. The Crimes Bill is so bad that the more there is heard of it, and the less it is liked. Sir GEORGE TREVELYAN, Liberal Unionist though he is, does not see how any true Liberal can vote for such a measure; and, as he speaks with special authority, his power- ful indictment against the Bill is' likely to have considerable influence on the situation. At Birmingham the Gladstornan Liberals have had a significant triumph. In the cen- tre division, which is represented by Mr. BRIGHT, there was a meeting on Thursday evening to elect forty-three representatives

to the To Thousand. The vacancies were filled by Gladstonians, who were elected by large majorities over " Unionists :" and, fol- lowing on this, a resolution was passed in condemnation of Coercion, and .in favour of local self-government for Ireland.- Mr. CHAMBERLAAN'S influence would seem to be on the wane in Birmingham, and it will decline elsewhere, if he does not show himself more consistent and coherent. He made two speeches at Ayr on Thursday. In the first, referring to the Round Table Conference, he said : One of my colleagues in that cenference, Sir William Vernon Harcourt, who is the lieutenant of Mr. Gladstone, and who was supp 3sed to represent his views at the conference, has told you that the conference disclosed the fact that the differemces between us are secondary and unimportant. I do not say they are secondary. I say they are funda- mental. In the second speech, Mr. CHAMBERLAMT delivered himself as follows :

I have never yet had an opportunity of talking lc a Gladstonian Liberal on this point without discov- ering that the differences between us vanish with discussion,; that while, on the one hand, we may each maintain the importance of our principles, when it comes to the application of them the differ- ences sink in,to insignificance. EMERSON says that a foolish consistency in little things is the hobgoblin of little minds. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN would seem to be deter- mined that a charge of foolish consistency I shall not stick to him ; but how if people should be driven to conclude that he is foolishly inconsistent? Ah, if he would but follow Sir Graoßoz TuEvaLYAN's example, and show that coercion is an " ever-failingl and ever poisonous remedy," ha would be himself again.

'Thomas McCormick, seem to have had "a ' regular set to*" last month, on Newton Corn- mon, in the presence of a large number of people. Sufficient evidence was not forth- coming to convict certain a,iders and abettors, and they were dischargA. The principals pleaded guilty, and were " let off," after being bound over for their good behaviour. Per- haps the magistrates thought they had been sufficiently " punished "; Anders had his foot injured in the contest, and lirtc,Cormitk was "bled until he became weak!' What glory! Who wouldn't be a prize fighter?

IPolice Constables Cameron and Hughes, of Earlestown, were badly injured on the 3rd instant whilst obeying .orders to eject two ruftl ins named Donoghue and Smith from the Wellington Hotel. Some of the crowd, strange to say, took part against the con- stables, who did their duty pluckily, and landed I their men, who are now lying in gaol— one getting six and the outer three months. Mr. W. S. Gilbert meant to be " kinder-sar- astic " when he said—'' The policeman's (lot is not a happy one ; " but as to this case, at any rate, it nits the nail on the head.

A. " Daily News " correspondent, refer- ring to the situation in Egypt, says that as soon as the shooting season com- mences Englishmen and non-descripts of all breeds go forth and tread down the crops of the natives. Crops ! Who cares about crops either in England, Ire- land, or Egypt, when it is a question of sport ? The natives ought to be glad to see so many fine gentlemen ; but somehow they are not pleased, and they make ptotest. There is nothing to be done with these Egyptians but spoil them as of old : they do not understand the blessings of civilisa- tion.

1 It appears that, for the past quarter, both the birth rate and the death rate are excep- tionally low in the Runcorn Union. Dr. Adartg old this was satisfactory as to deaths, and equally $o as to births; but this, as the Rev, f. L kwood jocularly remarked, was "from a doctor's' point of view." If the birth rate and death rate more evenly balanced each other generally, as in this instance, it would gltlainly be betier for the whole community. There Wa1.11'...1 t e leg' need to talk of emigration, or of the survi- val of the fittest in the struggle for exist- ence. But hov is this happy state of things to be brought about ? " Ay, there's the rub."

DIVI.TFI OF A WIDNES TRADESMAN.—Mr. John Forsyth, confactioner, of Waterloo-road, Widnes, who was a well- known chara,cter in the town, died on Thurs,lay morning. - DEATH 0, A RUNCORN TRADESMAN.—There was interred at Runcorn cemetery, on Wednesday afternoon, the mortal remains of Mr. James Shaw. formerly a furniture dealer in Bridge-street. Mr. Shaw, who had attained the age of 57 years, died unexpectedly on Good Friday, from coergestion of the lungs, after a very brief illness. A native of War- rington, he settled in Runcorn 26 years ago. and by zealous attention to business and commercial integrity and pru- dence, he raised himself to a position of affluence, being the owner of much property in the town, and a shareholder in several successful public concerns. MEMORIAL TO THE LATE CASON BATtcLAY, RANCOR/4- A large congregation assembled in Runcora Parish Church, on Saturday night, to witness the unveiling of a handsome reredos erected by Miss Barclay to the memory of her father the late vicar ef the parish.. Besides being a graceful tri- bute to the memory of a man who was universally respected and admired, the reredos gives additional beauty to the church, and se substantial an expression of her love to the church entitles the giver to the sincere gratitude of the parishioners. The reredos, which is from the art studio of Messrs. Norbury and Paterson, of Liverpool, is of alabaster relieved with coloured marble and jewels. (la the centre panel the Ascension is represented together with the em- blems of the four evangelists. In the side panels are sacred monograms; whilst carved on the border below is the fol- lowing inscription: —"Erected to the glory of God and in loving memory of John Barclay by his daughter Edith, Easter, 1887." The total cost of what is a most ornate de- coration to the chancel is upwards of £3OO. ItUNCORN FOOTBALL Om-I.—To-day the Runcorn first team journey to Bradford to play the famous club of that Sown. This will be the third Yorkshire team the club bare met in the course of six days, and it is unfortunate that through a series of casualties they cannot play their full I strength. With a weakene6l team they had to succumb to Leeds Parish Church, on Monday, but on Tuesday, with an even more disorganised team, they scored a meritorious victory against liallfax Free Wanderers. Both these teams were hospitably entertained to a capital dinner at Wilson's Hotel, the repasts being served in Mrs. Jackson's best style. On the latter day H. C. Speakman, an acknowledged c4e- brity in the centre three-quarter position, Wkitst following Iris employment at the Widnes Alkali Works, fell from a slightly raised platform, and his arm coming in contact with an earthenware pipe, was sniously cut at the wrist. Dr. McCarnbridge stitched and bandaged the wound, which is nicely healing. Mr. Riley wilt take his position to-day, whilst E. Lunt will go on the wing in place of Cawley. Mr. Wright is still unable to take his position forward, and a man will be drafted out of the second team to fill it.

RUNCORN CO-OPERLTIVE SOCIETY AIM TRE QUEEN'S JUBILEE.—A meeting of the members of the Runcorn Co- operative Society was held in the aesernbly roam on Tues- day evening, for the purpose of considering whether they should aid the local jubilee celebration by a donation. There were about 60 persons present, and Mr. D. Worthing- ton occupied the chair. Mr. Boardman (Widnes) asked whether, if anything was given, the money would be equally divided between Widnes and Runcorn, or would the Widnes members have to pay to come over the bridge in order to see Runcorn people rejoice with the money of the co-operators of Widnes. (Laughter.)—The Chairman objected to Mr. Boardman's remarks, and said he was the man who caused a disturbance at the last annual meeting. There were loud cries of " withdra bit the chairman did net respond to the demand.—Mr. lace advocated a contribu- tion towards a cottage hospital, which was an institution that would benefit Runcorn.—Mr. William Betuey sug- gested that if they wanted to be charitable, they could not Ido better than send a goad stun to the aid of the Cradley heath chainmakers, whose condition at the present time was a disgrace to Christian England. (Apolanse )—Even- Wally, on the proposition of Mr. William flolford, seconded by Mr. James Patin, it was decided, with only three dissen- tients, that the society make no contribution towards the jubilee fund.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
Another attempt to kill the Czar. Poor fellow! He has tried Coercion for many years; but it is not proving to be good for either him or his people.

It must be very trying for John Bright to receive the thanks of the Tories for his "magnificent efforts." " Tis strange ; tis passing strange ; tis pitiful; tis wondrous pitiful; '' and—well, what Liberal does not warm at the name of Bright? So let it end there.

It is stated that, owing to previous engage- ments, Mr. Chamberlain will not be present in the House to VOW for the second reading- of the Coercion Bill. Perhaps other Liberal Unionists will find themselves prevented from voting by similar accidents. What a happy accident it would be if the Bill 'should fail, after all' to stain the statute book!

The Liberal UniconiStS a Aberdeen have been inviting Sit Ot:-.orge Trevelyan to ad- dress than; but they have received such a letter from him that the invitation is aropped. Sir George says he has "the greatest objec- tions to the proposals of the Government to pass penal clauses which can be used for the suppression of the National League and Nationalist Press." And so say all of us. By-the-by, would it not be as well to invite the ex-Irish Secretary to an anti-Coercion meeting—to a meeting of real Unionists?

Colonel King-Harman, who has been ap- pointed Irish Under-Secretary, knows some- thing of Ireland, and Ireland knows some- thing of him. He is one of the rack-renters, and the Land Commissioners had to make enormous reductions in his rent last Novem- ber. Even the "Times" thinks there are other Irishmen "better fitted for the post," while the " Standard " admits that the ap- pointment has " caused some surprise even to the friends of the Government." It must be very pleasant to be thus damned by the faintest of faint praise; but he deserves it all.

Widnes seem o to be improving, or pet- haps it would be better to say, growing. It transpired at the meeting of the Local Board, on Tuesday, that a rate of as id in the pound, which was estimated to realise £10,225, had actually produced .£10,490. The increase is not a great deal, but it is better than a decrease; for it shows that the town, afier the depression in trade, is looking up.

It was suggested at the vestry meeting of the Warrington Parish Church that it would be a good thing in the Jubilee year to take down the churchyard wall and re-build it. The Warrington mind seems to run on walls this year. The Jubilee Committee have resolved by way of celebration to knock •down a wall in Sankey street. The inhabitants mast take care, or outsiders will be speaking of them as wall-eyed.

It was a "happy thought" to treat the wives and children of the Warrington Volun- teers to a tea at the Drill Hall. The wives have a share of the burden in being left to themselves whilst their husbands are drilling and marching and shooting, and should have a share of the entertainment. "Smoking Concerts" for the men may be good; but tea and sandwiches for women and children are better; they are substantial creature comforts, and are no worse in that they do eta end in smoke.

Certain "society" ladies in America have been having "a Greek dinner " as the latest novelty. "The guests," it is stated, "sat on great chairs covered with rugs, and each wore a wreath of laurel tied with purple ribbon. The menu was written in Greek, and among the dishes were wild boar, roast kid, and hare." It is a pity these fair Americans with so little to do didn't add "calf's head" and "gooseberry fool" to the menu. Perhaps they will come to think of it as appropriate by-and-by.

They are a favoured people at St. John's, ERrlestown ; they always have a lively.time of it at the Easter vestry meeting. The Vicar, the Rev. T. R. Matthews, has been in many a row, as our readers will remember. He insinuated, on Monday, that one of his parishioners knew more of the law than the gospel; and the parishioner was not slow to retort. Hard words were flying more than once during the meeting, but fortunately no bones were broken.

When it was proposed that a voluntary church rate should be levied of twopence in the pound, Mr. Corlett said he believed in people going to church and paying their own rate. Tnis is dangerous doctrine, surely— in the mouth of a Churchman, It is alto- gether too suggestive of a regard for religious eqtrtlity ; and when Churchmen begin to entertain ideas of this kind there is no saying where it will end. What if they were to take to thinking that every religions tub should stand on its own bottom—that Church and State should be separated ? Have a care, Mr. Corlett; you are in " a parlous state."

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The last meeting of this Board, as at present constituted, was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present Mr. John ,Weir (vice-chairman), the Revs. J. Lockwood and J. W. N. Tanner; Messrs. Warburton, Parr Aaron. Jackson, Hamilton. Wallington, Mclntyre, Hadfield, Hewitt, Stokes. Lewis, tirandreth, Forster, Fisher, Highfield, Monnfield, and LI. Linaker (clerk).

MISCELLANEOUS. A letter was read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the payment to Mr. Linaker of the sum of £35 for his services as clerk to the School Attendance Com- mittee during the past year.—Letters were, read from vari- ous &Bejaia of the Board asking that the usual allowance of money be granted them in lieu of beer, and it was decided that beer to, allowed, or money in lieu tbereof.—The tenders of ,the following persons for the supply of drapery, boots and shoes, and clothing, were accepted:—Drapery, Mr. Wright, Halton; boots and shoes, Mr. Hobson, Manchester; clothing, Mr. Jones, Runcorn.

div.p: EASTER VESTRY MEETINGS.
ST. MICHAEL'S. DITTON.

On Thursday night, at the annual Easter vestry meting the vicar, the Rev. C. W. Woolf presiding, the accounts for the past year were preented, and showed a balance in hand of Is 3d. The Vicar appointed Mr. A. E. Smith as his warden, and Mr. Samuel Evans was elected people's warden. The sidesmen are as follows :—.A. G. Kyle, F. Bergl, R. Glover,Josepti Longton, John Lucaa, and R. Lewis. Messrs. Lewis and Longton were appointed rari-decanal represen- tatives.

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

Last evening, the Runcorn Parish vestry meeting was held, the Rev. E. M. Wood, vicar, occupying the chair. The accounts were passed; Mr. Lake was appointed vicar's warden, and Mr. W. Whittaker parishioners' warden. Sides- men were elected as follows :—Messrs M. Barker W. Mel- lor, Henry White, and J. R. Meredith (appointed by Mr. Lake), and Messrs George Moss, W. Timmins, E. Marwood, and E. A. Chorlton (appointed by the meeting). The ques- tion of making the church free and open was next discussed at some length. The chairman said he was strongly in favour of free seats, and a motion to this effect was carried by 27 votes to 12. We bold over a faller report of the pro. ceedings. ' _

div.head: GRATEFUL CLERGYMAN.
div.p: A GRATEFUL CLERGYMAN.

The following sincere and earnest letter from the Rev. I Thomas J. Bryant appeared in the "Primitive Methodist World" for March 24th. As it touches a subject of universal impertAnce, we cheerfully give it place In our columns:—

div.head: --- To the Editor of the "Primitive 'Methodist World."
div.p: --- To the Editor of the "Primitive 'Methodist World."

Sir,—l wish to call attention, through your inflwietial journal,to the wonderful merits of a mailicine of which I have received practical proof over and over again for a num- ber of years past. It has never disappointed me, but bas always been productive of good results, having restored many people who have been abandoned as incurable. For the benefit of those who are suffering from diseases of the liver and kidneys, or from general debility,/ ask space far the publication of the following statement. Some yeare ago I was stationed in Canada, and while there nay attention was repeatedly called to the great bensfit SOTIEI members of my congregation derived frosn the use of War-let's SAFE Cure. The cases were under my own obser- vation to a large extent, and although somewhat biased in .my opinion of patent medicines, I was forced to acknow- ledge this one as being one of the best general remedies which we have for popular use. Some of the cases et sick- ness which I saw on my pastoral visits showed a recovery where medical aid had apparently proved unsuccessful. I had only been in Canada a short time, when (o wing to the severity of the winter climate, and the great amount of extra labour which devolved upon me in conducting ray pastoral woes) I was taken severely ill, with pains in my back and loins, water high coloured, with a large quantity of brick-duet sediment (uric acid) in the bottom of the ves- sel. My trouble was almost entirely confined to the kid- neys, and the organs were very much disordered, as evi- denced by the suffering which I endured. Mrs. Bryant and myself concluded that we would try Warner's SAVE Cure, and are now very thankful that we did so, for I had only used a small quantity before I was delighted to find the astonishioe recuperative effect it was having upon me, and I soon recovered. In July, 1883, I returned to England, and for fear that I should not be able to procure the remedy . .

in this country. I brought a large supply with me, for my- self and wife, the latter having alao received great benefit from its use. I have recommended its use very largely in this country in a greaty many cases. an 1 in every instance with the best pessible results, PO far as I know. I may mention Mrs. Coe, of Lichpool Farm, Horsham, to whom Mrs. Bryant recommended the medicine, as well as Mrs. Puttock and het two daughters, all of whom were cured after having been ill for a long time with chronic difficulties incidental to women. _

I consider Warner's SATE Cure one of the most remark- able medicines for diseases of the liver and kidneys, and am such a believer in its virtues, that I cordially and earnestly advise all your readers who are ill to immediately begin its use, confident that it will not disappoint their most sanguine expectations. Yours truly. 30, Barrin,gton-road, Horsham, Sussex.
(Rev.) Tacoma J. BRuarr.
