kick, and sending the oval to the Oldham 25. The Oldham forwards rushed the ball up the field, a scrimmage being formed near centre, Mambas saving. Barnes got in a nice run and pass, and shortly afterwards leaked like scoring. He next took a drop at goal, a minor resulting. Mills kicked off. but there was no return, and the same player passed to Smith, who kicked to Speakman, who replied to centre. Nolan now obtained possession, and put in a run to 25, the Warrington forwards relieving, Adamson collaring Walkden with the ball. The Oldham forwards, by good play, next compelled Speakman to touch down. From the kick out Wbittle returned to touch. Fair Turner and E. Dillon, from tbe line out, put in a good mak to the Oldham quarters. Whittle now saved well, and Antrobns tackled Nolan in fine style. A free kick was next acceded to Speakman for off-side play, scrimmages taking place in the centre. Whittle passed to Barnes, who, in tarn, re-passed to Antrobus, and the trio dribbled up the field; Baines get- ting over and Frank Turner failing atgoal. The Warrington forwards quickly worked the oval to the 25, and Lund, by a strong kick, scored another minor for the home team. Barnes returned the kick out, and the same player put in a good kick, and Cragan, obtaining possession, took the ball up the field. Wild and Nolan took the play to the Warrington quarters, bat ttie forwards relieved, Play being of a fluctua- ting and give-and-take character until half-time was called. The second half of the game was very keenly contested, Oldham playing against the wind, their defence being splen- did. Try as they did the Warringtonians could not again score. Barnes and Massey were particularly prominent; Nolan, for the visitors, playing a good defensive game ; and when the referee blew his whistle the score stood—War- rington 1 try arta 5 minors to 6 minors for the visitors. On behalf of the borne team it may be stated that Speakman displayed good judgment. The three-quarters played an excellent game, Barnes in particular being very prominent. his short kicks and following up being much admired. The two half-backs were always there when wanted, and all the forwards worked well together and played a grand combined game. For the visitors Nolan, Smith, Walkden, and Wild were the pick of a good lot. _ .

WARRINGTON CA/110LIC UNITED F.C. v. DALLAN BREW. 311 T.—The above teams met for tbe return match on Satar- day, on the ground of the former, which resulted in a victory for United by two tries, four minors to two minors. T. Lynne and Kenealy played,well for United. WMNES Y. HORBURY.—This match was played at Wid- nes on Monday. Horbury kicked off, and after a lot of loose scrimmaging Harding followed up and scored a try for Widnes. Shortly afterwards Morris received a pass from Howard, and dropped a beautiful goal from h diffi- cult position. Smith and Hardman each got over, but owing to informality tho ball had to be brought back, and nothing further was done up to bait time. Directly after the change of ends Nettleton scored a goal from a free kick, and a dead bail was notched a moment subsequently to the Yorkshiremen. Here the Widnes men pulled them- selves together, and Fogg, Hardman, and Smith passed cleverly, the last-named running from the half-way flag and grounding, but Kiddie missed the „major point. 'Fogg got in immediately afterwards, but the try was disallowed. This was followed by a minor to Horburv. Coming away on the loose, Howard dribbled over, Kiddie again failing at the place, and another minor fell to Horbary. Smith here put in a grand ran to Horbury 25, and no side ar- rived, Widnes winning by one goal and three tries to one geal. Sr. lisrans v. Wireans.—/These teams met at St. Helens on Good Friday. The afternoon was fine, and the game was witnessed by about three thousand spectators. The game was very fast and well contested. In the first half the Saints had decidedly the beet of the game, the Widnes turn not appearing to have the slightest chance. At the call of half time the score was St. Helens two tries and lye minors to Widnes one minor. The tries were obtained by Finney and Basnett, but the places being difficult ones, the kicks at goal failed. In the second half the visitors seemed determined if possible to change the aspect of the game, and went off with a-great rush, but the home team was equal to the occasion, and pitying with good combina- tion succeeded in frustrating any serious attempt upon their goal line. After about twenty minutes play in this half from a splendid run by Smith. Plumpton gat posses- sion of the oval, and grounded behind the postsethis being the first tangible point for the visitors. The place kick, although a comparatively easy one, failed. In the and the game resulted in a victory for the home team, the score being as follows :—St. Helens, two tries and seven minors, Widnes one try and three minors. The teams were : St. Helens—Tickle, hack; Haseldnn, Halton. and Foreman. three-quarter backs; Finney and Andrews, bait-backs; Bortlawick (captain), McLoughlin' Basnett, Harwood, Pen- nington, Ellison, Leatherbarrow, Marsh, and Dearden, for- wards. Widnes—S. Biogham, back; Barker, Plumpton, and Parkinson, three-quarter backs; Howard and Wilkinson, balf backs; Keddie (cap'ain), Smith, Hardman, Woods, Fogg, Wright', Spencer' Williams, and Barber; forwards. Rateconw. V. LEEDS Penner Clunteer.—Comicg on from Aspull, where they played a drawn game, the laseds Parish Church turned up at Runcorn to play the famohs wearers of the green. The home team Were abort of Cawley. Wright, ' and Clarke, and of course were not seen at their best. The weather was beautifully fine, but the powerful sun acted as a deterrent to good play. Leeds kicked off, and Davies re- tamed, but the Parish invaded the Runcorn territory, and, after scene give-and-take play, the home tearer conceded a minor. Speakman dropped out, and Broady transferred to Wainwright, who made 3 grand run three-parts the length , of the field, and crossed the line, Broady failing at the place. The Church forwards took the ball up the field, and it was kicked over the line, and Turner dropped on it and ' scored for them. The place kick did not corns off. This was all of moment up to half time. On facing about, W. Hughes started the ball, and the play was mostly of a for- ward nature for some time, the visitors showing the beat form. From a scrimmage in Runcorn 25, Wilson got bold, and, passing to Davy, the lasbnamed dropned the ball beau- tifully over the bar,the same side afterwards scoring a minor, leaving them winners of a pleasant game by a goal, a try, and two touches down, against a try and one touch down. Teams ;—Leeds Path*: Church: Back, J Northend ; three- quarter-backs, G Blackburn, A Davy, and Stewart; half backs, H B Hernmons and W Watson; forwards F Coope, B Dickinson, G Greenwood, S Green, J Helliwsll, Robin- son, Ackroya, J W Madtey, and It F Turner. Runcorn: Back, T Woods; three-quarter backs, H C Speakman. T Davies, and W A Riley; half backs, H Hughes and H G Andrews; forward., W H Broady, J Ford, W Hughes, W Faulkner, J Lewis, P Riley, J Barns, G Wainwright, and Galley. HGNCORN v. HALIFAX FREE WANDERERS —Played RE Runcorn on Tuesday evening, before a fair number of spec- tators. As the visitors had to depart by an early train only a short game of 25 minutes each way was played. Although short of Speakman. Andrews, and Cawley behind, and Wright and Lewis, forward, the local team exhibited far better form than on the previous day against Leeds Parish Church, and having the best of the scrimmages both in the pack and the loose, the game was a very fast and exciting one. Shortly after the start Wainwright took a neat pass from Davies, and made a strong run half the length of the field, and being brought rip passed amongst the forwards. Clarke getting hold, completed a meritorious piece of work by getting over the line. Broady failed at goal. Two mi- nutes later Wainwright dropped a beautiful goal, and Run- corn, by mune of Engle capital short passing, continued to PTeag the visitors, and were several times very dangerous. .At half time the score was : Runcorn, 1 goal, 1 try, and 1 dead ball to Halifax nil. In the second half the visitors bad the wind in their favnnr, and had rather the beet of the play, but the Runcorn defence was very good, Woods play- ing a sterling game at back. Davies relieved on several occasions by splendid rune, and Runcorn were once or twice within an ace of scoring. The remelt was—Rancorn, a goal, a try, and a minor, to Halifax four minors. Teams: Hali- fax Free Wanderers—Beck, B Itaywood ; three-quarter backs, J H Hitchen, J J Howard, C W Collard; half backs. S Honfall and J Lodge; forwards, C Taight, J Turner, H Gibson, W Wilson, L E Thornton, R Walker, E King, A W Bates. Runcorn—Back, T Woods; three-quarter backs T Davies, W Riley, and E Lunt; half backs. H Hughes and Whitby; forwards, W H Broady, J Ford, W Hughes, W Faulkner, P Riley, J Clarke, .1 Barns, G Wain- wright, and J Getley. WARRINGTON ("A" TEAM) v. WIDNES BECREATION (IST rEAY.—The return fixture between these teams was played at Wayrington on Saturday, before a large flambe, of spectators. Widnes had a strong team, whilst Warring- ton played aix 2nd team men. Noon kicked off for Wid- nes at 340, and tinsworth not making a very good return the ball was scrimmaged in centre. The visiting forwards broke awiv with a eril ble taking play to to the home 25, Jones saving nie.elV. __Hackett relieved by a short dribble,

The teams were as follows :—Warrington : Back, W Speakman ; three-quarters, Massey, Barnes, and Lund; half backs, Whittle and Antrobus ; forwards, Fair Turner, Frank Turner, Povey, E Dillon, Littlewood, Cragan, Davies, Adamson, and Ashton (captain). Oldham: Back, Walkden ; three-quarters, Smith, Mills, and Simpson; half backs, No- :an and Wyatt; forwards. the Brothers Woolatencroft, Rhodes, Taylor, Thwaites, Wood, Halkyard, E Wild, and IVhit.head. Umpires, Messrs Barnes and Hulme. Referee, Mr Trevor Smith, Manchester. Nolan, Wild, and Simpson were from the Rochdale Hornets.

WARViIIiteTON V. OLDEII3I. The return march between the Warrington and Oldham clubs was played at Warrington on Monday afternoon, in beautiful weather, IP the presence of about 8 000 'persons. Frank Turner kicked off, the bait going into touch. • Scrim- mages then took place in the centre, Lund putting in a good

I ton lines, and H. Dawson made a splendid attempt to score from behind the pack, when he was tackled by Coop. It then fell to Massey from some loose play to relieve by a strong kick. The Wakefield forwards, however, were slightly better in the pack, and again pressed the home team to their lines, where a dead ball nee registered to the visitors. Coop dropped the bill out, and Barnes, Dillon, and Davies rushed through to mid-field. Lowrie secured at this point, and after a splendid run be was tackled by Fair Turner at quarter flag. H. Dawson pat is a smart run, rind nearly scored, but was brought up. Colley, having secured in a loose scrimmage, made a drop at goal, but the ball fell short, and Coop made a fair catch. lhe ball fell into the hands of tha Tr nity men, who agaia carried hostilities to the Warrington quarter. Coley again made a drop at goal, but the ball fell short, and Coop made a secopd fair catch. His kick was improved moon by Dillon and Ashton, but the advantage was only maintained for a few minutes. H Dawson rushed the.ball to the line, and was only brought down at the corner flag by Massey. I Coop soon afterwards had to concede a touchdown. Coop dropped out, and the ball, after a loose scrimmage, was car- ried into touch. Ross threw in, and Harrison cirried the ball over the line. Hamshaw failed at goal. On the bill being brought out Dunne passed to Fallas. The latter neatly passed to Ash, who got over the line, but being tackled by Lund a maul ensued, fr am which a touchdown resulted. Some good loose play, in which Warrington showed up in good form, fol- lowed the drop out, and some good' dribbling by Povey. Ashton, and Fair. Turner carried the game into the Wakefield half. Hamehaw saved well, but Speakman stayed his progress. Wakefield had now to give way to a strong and combined forward attack, bet Hamshaw's returns were sure and his kicks safe. At the call of time, Wakefield Trinity bad wen by three tries and six minors to Warring- ton one minor. Team e:—Wakefield Trinity : H 0 Harnshaw, back; F Ash, H Fal las, and Colley, three-quarter backs ; H Dawson (captain) and R Dunce, half-backs ; J Nathan, F Ross, P Booth, H Whiteley, F Lourie, J Gomersall, A Thompson, J Dawson, Harrison, forwards. Warrington : Coop (Totting- ton), back; Massey, Barnes. and Lund, three-quarter backs; Speakman and Antrobus, half-backs; H Ashton (captain). Fair Turner, E Dillon. Frank Termer, J Jolley, W Povey, R Littlewood, W Hayes, Davies, forwards. Umpires: Mr T B Parry (Wakefield), Mr Barnes (Warrington.) Referee, Mr A T Kemble, Liverpool.
PARISH CHURCH.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 16s 1887 EASTER VESTRY MEETINGS. WARRING FON. ST. ANN'S. The vestry meeting of this church was held on Tuesday morning, the Rev. J. G. Richards presiding. There were also present—Messrs. John Baird, Janie s Baird, E. Gibbon, G. Armstrong, E. Dagnall, P. Randall, and Woods (vestry clerk.)—The Chairman nominated Mr. G. Armstrong as vicar's warden, and Mr. B. F. Robinson was elected , people's warden—Messrs. James Baird and E. Gibbon were j re-elected sidemen, and Messrs. John Baird and G. Arm- strong were appointed lay representatives at the ruri- decanal conference.—This was all the public business. HOLY TRINITY. The vestry meeting of Holy Trinity was held in the church on Tuesday evening. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton presided, and there were also present Messrs. John Hatton, R. W. Rowson, Wm. Harrison, Harding, Westvrell, and A. Brimelow. The statement of accounts was submitted by Mr. Hutton (vicar's warden), and showed that the total re- ceipts during the year, including a balance from last year of £32 12s 7d, was £22T es 81. The total expenditure had been £2O 17s 6d, leaving a balance in hand of £lB 9s 2d.1 It was explained, however, that accounts were owing amounting to over £3O. The accounts were passed.—The Chairman re-appeiuted Mr. John Hatton as his warden, and Mr. R. W. Rowson was re•elecud people's warden. Messrs. E. Booth, R. Dobson, jtrnr., J. Haltom James Hard- ing were elected eidesmen ; Messrs. Charles White and James Fairclough lay delegates ; and Mr, H. B. White vestry clerk.—A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the proceedings to a close. ST. PAUL'S. The annual vestry meeting in connection with St. Paul's Church, Bewsey-road, was held on Monday morning, the vicar, the Rev. S. Wilkinson in the chair. Amongst those also present were the Rev. R. Wood Samuel (carate), Ald- erman Sutton and Mr. T. Jolley (churchwardens), Messrs D. W. Finney, Jeans, Lawton, Bebbingtom &c.—Ahlerrnan Sutton, in giving a statement of accounts, said that at St. Paul's they commenced the year with a balance due to the wardens of £22 12s 91. Church expenses during the year had amounted to £ tl2 7s, which, added to the balance in favour of the wardens, made a total expenditure of £134 19s 9d. The income for pew rents had been £24 Ige 100, as against 315 17e lld last year, and from Sunday evening collections £B5 He 00. as against £lOB 51 6d last year. In all the income had been £l3l 18 sel, leaving a balance due to the wardens of £3 18s old. Every year,. he re- marked, the parish was getting poorer, and it required much energy and care to make the income meet the expenditure. He thought that the parishioners had come out handsomely, and that they might congratulate themselves that they stood so well at the end of the year...—Mr. T. Jolley also expreseed satisfaction with the condition of affairs.—The Vicar remarked that during the last feWvears, locluding the money spent on St. Barnabas, a great deal had been collected in that perish, and during the last few years they had spent something like £lO,OOO. He also wished to allude to another work—the erection of a new mission church for Bewsey at a cost of £750, generously given by Sir Gilbert Greenall. He hoped that the church, when erected, would be a great hies- sing to the neighbourhood. During the year a great work had' been done in the restoration of the churchyard, and many thanks were due to those who had helped to raise the money required. The Vicar then nominated Mr. T. Jolley as his churchwarden.—On the proposition of Mr. Finney, secon- ded by Mr. J. Behhington, Alderman Sutton was re-elected' people's warden, and the wardens were heartily thanked for their past services. Messrs Ashurst, T. Morris, W. Pollitt, W. Lawless,. J. Smethurst, and D. Jones were appointed sidemen.

The annual vestry meeting of the parish of Warrington was held in the vestry at toe Parish Church on Tuesday at noon. The Rev. J. A. lirummend (curate) presided, and amongst those also present were the Rev. T. H. Twissa the Ref: Morley Stevenson, and Messrs. R. W. Francomb, N. B: Percival, J. Dewhurst. Alderman Webster, J. E. Wright, Stringer, W. triggle, H. B. White (vestry clerk), &c. —The Chairman said that the Rector (the ii ey. W. Quekett) bat for several'dievs been confined to his bed through ill- ness, and was in is somewhat critical state. Otherwise he would have been at the meeting.—Mr. Percival gave a statement of the accounts, from which it appeared that the receipts for the year amounted to £275 19s 2d. The ex- penditure having been £275 15s 7d, there was a balance in hand of '.3e Tel. The voluntary church rate had realised £3O 194 3d. The liabilities outstanding this year were £74 9e, as compared with -.263 33 731 la.at year. This year the churchwardens' offertory had been less than the previous year, and the Rector's, more, The churchwarden's offertory last year amounted to £246 193 61, and this year it was £217 5s Ild a while the Rector's offertory last year was £l2le7s 81, and this year it was £136 le sd. Out of that sum the Rector had given £67 12s to charitable institutions. The accounts were then nassed.—The Chairman, on behalf of the Rector, appointed Mr. Percival to act as Recter'S warden, and Mr. R. W. Francomb was elected peo- ple's warden. Mr, J. Deialaurst and Mr. W. Gill were ap- pointed sielesmen.—Me. Wright asked what had been done with the fund arising from the old alms hotrses. Two years ago be and Mr. Prancomb distributed it, and he had not heard of it being distributed since. He did not see why the money, which was lying in Parr's bank, should te allowed to accumulate. Mr. Percival replied that he and Mr. Firth- comb would look, into the matter.—On the proposition of Mr Peecival, a voluntary church rate of 3d in the £ was laid.— Messrs. Webster and Boakton were, on the proposition of : Mr. E. Wright, seconded by Mr. Dewlaurst, appointed lay delegates to the diocesan conference, and Mr. H. B. White was, on the motion of Mr. Percival, re-elected vestry Danshurst proposed a vote of thanks to the churchwardens for- the wait year, and suggested that the wall facing Church-place should be repaired. The church yard might also be put in better repair, and there might be new trees planted—Alderman Webster, who seconded the proposition, said that it incurred to him that something of a special nature might be undertaken in this, the Jubilee, year. He admitted the nscessity of re-building the war:- mentioned, but it, had occurred to him that they might undertake the re•hanging of the bells.—Mr: Wright said he should like to see the wall repaired as soon as possible, as that was an absolute neees,ity, but he thought that they would not yet be able to carry out Alderman Webster'e sug- gestion. The preposition was then carried.—ln reply to Mr. Stringer, who mentioned a person having been rensested to leave an appropriated seat,Mr Francomb said that he had been people's warden for three years, and he thought that if there was a chuseti in the country where the poor ware considered more than anyone else it was at that church. As soon as it was time to commence service he never considered any seats appropriated. If people were not in by then the seats were tilled up. He did not think there was much room. for complaint, but if there was a complaint it should be mede to the churthsvardens.—The meeting then 200- clud ed. •

CHRIST CHURCH, LATCHFORD. The vestry. meeting in connection with this church was held in tbe school-roam, pn, Thursday evening. lha Rev. B. B. Prescott presided, and there was a fair attendance of parishioners. The statement of accounts was submitted by ,Mr. H. Woods, the vicar's warden, and showed that at the I 'beginning of the year just closed there was a balance due to the churchwardens of £l6 13s Sidornd that the I receipts during the year had been £l9l 8s 4d. After meet- ing the expenditure there was still a balanceo due to the churchwardens of .216,468 d and, Mr. Woods explained, there were other outstanding liabilities which brought the adverse balance up to about £3O. The number of coins received at the offertories during the past year was 10,627, an increase of 142,• over the previous year. Mafia were, made up as follows:—One bank note, nine sove- reigns, 30 half-sovereigns, one crown, 115 half- crowns, 102 florins, 0843 shillings, 1,711, sixpence, 1,655 threepence% 3.7.60 pennies, 2,512 half-pennies, and four farthings. Alll3ough the number of coins receiyeid during the year had increased by 148 over the number, received during, the previous year, yet the total amount of the offertories was about £l5 lees, thereby showing that more people gave, but that the offerings its each individual case were less. The charchwardens-wiehed to„publicly thank the ladies of the CharchwOrkers' Association for the valuable assistance they had, so freely givers during the past year. They bad given the substantial donation of £l5 towards the church accounts, and that had enabled the wardena to present so favourable a balance sheet as they bad done. (Hear, hear.)—On the motion of Mr. W. Starkey, seconded by Mr. S, Davies, the accounts were passed.—The Chairman then again appointed Dir. H. Woods to be vicar's warden for the ensuing year; and on the motion. of Mr. Gorton. seconded by Mr. Coxon, Mr. John Lee was Ve-elected parishioner's wardom—The .question a,l to whether it would be advisable to have offer— tories at the church every Sunday evening instead of only on one Sunday evening in the month. was then discussed. it seemed to be tho general opinion that there ought to be- es offertory every Sundaypening, and that this would be the best way to make the income of the church meet the expenditure without outside help. It was ultimately unani- mously decidQd, on the motion of, Councillor Greenalls seconded by Mi. Gorton, that the churchwardens be recom- mended to conolder the advisability of having offertories every Sunday evening.—Mr. Lee then nominated Mr. Gor- ton as his, sidesman. and Mr. Woods nominated Mr.. Coxon to a similar office.—Mr. John White and, Mr. James Lowe were re•elected lay delogates to the ruri-decanal conference. It was also agreed that the organist's Salary should again. be £2O for the year, with a gratuity of £lo.—Mr. Stadtey at this point referred to the choir treat, and said he thought when the choir were taken away they ought to be taken away in something like fisst. class style), and not stinted in the way they had been, hav- ing to pay for their own tea..—Some discussion took plac-a on this subject, in the course of whiola the sees-ices and efficiency of the choir were highly spoken of, and it was generally conceded that they ought to be liberally treated on the occasion of their trip.—The Chairman remarked that he hoped that the next time the congregation was asked to subscribe towards the treat of the choir there would be a mote liberal response.—The verger's salary was fixed at £5, with a gratuity of £l.—Votes of thanks were, then passed to jibe choir. to the Rey. J. B. Prescott, and to the ladies of , the Churchworkers' Association. In moving the vote of thanks to the Churchworkere Association, Mr. Lee men- tioord that in addition to the £l5, they bad given towards the churchwarden's expenses, they had on many previous occasions handed over considerable sums of money. (Hear, hear.)-.-.A vote of thanks to the chairman concludedi the pi oceedings.

ST. JAMES'S, LATCHFORD. The annual vestry meeting of this church was held in the emery at neon on Monday. The vicar (the Rev. F. Slater) ' presined, and there were also present—Messrs, Hutchinson and Taylor, churchwardens; J. Worrell, 0, Andrews, J. Bolton, T. Walton, C.:S. Burgess, T. Jackson, and J. Debston.l 'e statement of the accounts was read by Mr. Ilatchinetne.l and showed that the total income for the year had been ' £749 17s Id, and after meeting expenditure there was a I balance in hand of 23 61.—Mr. C. S. Burgess asked if there 1 were any outstanding accorents.—Mr. Hutchinson replied , that there were a few, amounting in all to £l3 4s 24, He , thought the report was a satisfactory one, and showed them to be in a better positien than they bad been for some years. —On the motion of Mr. Worrell, seconded by Mr. Andrews, the accounts were passed.-7 The Chairman expressed heal acknowleJgments of the 3ervices el Mr. Hutchinson as the 1 vicar's warden during the' past year. During the year they; had progressed in many ways, and the accounts were in a more satiefactery position than they had been for a great • many years. Mr. Hutchinson had, bovrever, expressed a wish to retire from the poeition of churchwarden, and he (the chairman)' would therenore nominate Mr. C. S. Burgess , as his warden for the ensuing year.—Mr. Burgess having expressed his willingness to act as cherchwarden, said he scarcely agreed with the chairman as to the satisfactory position of the cherele finances. He wee/of-opinion that the expenses of the church should he paid out of the offertories I without falling back upon extraneous soureetr. Oh the pre- ViONEI day there were 290 commenicants in the church, a record which would Sear comparison with any`chierch in Warrington, and wits a communicant roll like that they 1 ought to be able to gat in the cTertories at least fat a year more than they were getting,. A penny a Sunday extra from 240 people would raise the additional Lite and 1 be might mention to there that if the offertory was raised to £l5O a veer the vicar would be willieg to receive one half instead of two-thirds.—Mr. Bolton was then elected people's i warden in place of Mr. Taylor, who wished to retire.—Ael the sidesmen, Messrs. Jachscn and Worrell, were nominated 1 by Mr. Burgess; and Meaars. Tauranac and Hollowell bY 1 Mr. Bolton.—As diocesan representatives Messrs. H. lrough- ton and C. S. Burgess were appointed, and Mr. Abreast was re-elected vestry clerk.---A vote of thanks to the chair- man concluded the proceedings. ST. THOMAS', STOCKTON 7-IEATIL The annual Ender vestry for this parish was held in.the vestry of St. Thomas' Church, on Tuesday, the Vicar, the': Rev. T. S. Tolle, presiding. Mr. E. W. Wools (people's warden) presented the annual etatement of accounts, from which it transpired that the total receipts were £233 us Ed. After meeting expendi- ture there was a balance due to the churchwardens of £lO 2s Bd. The year was commenced with a balance due to the churchwardens of £34 Os 11d, so that there was an improve- ment this year to the extent oeabout £24. (Hear, hear.),l 00 the proposition of Mr. :lobed Davits, seconded by Mr. Welsby, the aecounts were then passed. —The Chairman said that Mr. R. I. Wynne Jones, who had kindly acted as his warden, had left the parisle, and it became necessary for him to appoint someone e15e...1 He was glad to say that Mr. Robert Davies had kindly cob- I santed to act, and he (the chairman) had great nleasure in nominating him as his watden for the ensuing year. Mr. Ee W. Woods was re-elected people's warden, and Messrs. D. Logan, Wright, J. Laithwaite, J. a Calvert, and J. H. Sponceley were appointed sidesmen. Messrs. Woods and Tinsley were re-elected lay representatiees to attend the Ruridecanal• Conference.—A vote of thanks to the Chairman I brought the meeting to a close. GREAT SANKEY. The annual vestry meeting was held on Monday even- I ing. The 'Zing-, the Rev. E. S. Jackson, who presided at the outset of the meeting, stated that for the 51 See/days since.last Easter there had been 18,152 attendances in the morning, and 13,276 attendances in the evening. There had been 696, week-day attendances, and 712 communi- cants. The averages were : Morning 356 attednances, even- ing 260, and week-day 166. The year had been an eventful one in the way of restoration.—Mr. T. Owen, one of thei churchwardens, read particulars of the contingent fund, or evening colleetion, which, he said, was commenced at the Easter Vestry of 1884. it bad proved a very useful aid to the wardens to enable then) to cover extra expenditure that had become necessary for the comfort and convenience of the parishioners. 3 had been voted to the mortuary ac- count for repairs, but the great work of the year had been the removal of the gallery front, re-seating of the same, and pro-aiding a good entrance. Th s work had been accom- plished, and almost paid for.. During the year these • evening colleotiens had numbered 48, and realised £51.1 11i 57,e1, and there were subscriptions paid and promised to the amount of £43i The harvest festival collection realised MI 48 7d. After the expenditure of the year, there was a balance owing on this account of £39 19s 51d. The- ordinary aceeunts of the church showed a balance in hand of £9 odd, The accounts were auproved.—The Chairman' appointed Mr. Ames Davidson vicar's warden, and Mr. W. Hatton was selected as people's warden. Messrs. W. Skelton, Owen,. Bate, J. Baker, and Forster were eleonad sidesmen, and Mesere. T. Owen and Jeans lay representa- fives.- Mr. R. Boardman was re-appointed sexton. This was all the businees. CHRIST CHURCH, CROFT. The annual Easter vestry meeting of the parishioners was held on Monday morning. There were present the Rev. T. I'. Kirkman (rector), and Messrs. Richard Turner and Alfred Dixon (churchwardens), John leeinteth, James McCarthy, and Edward Monks. The Rector presided. The church. wardens Dresented their accounts, showing a balance in , their hands on Eastee Monday, 1887, of £3 19s B.fed The I chairman reappointed Mr. Turner as his warden. inn Dion was reappointed pariehieners' warden. A discussion took place with regard to the appointment of sexton and the funeral fees, and it was ultimately decided that lists of the funeral charges be printed, and that the sexton give a re- ceipt for the amount charged at each funeral, containing full particulars of the same. Mr. Monks was then reap- pointed sexton at a salern of £3 per annum, subject tu quarter'e notice on either side, and the salary to be paid quarterlya

div.head: WARRINGTON V. MANNINGHAM.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. MANNINGHAM.

The Warrington team journeyed to Manningharn on Saturday, to play their first fixture with this noted Club. Thanks to Mr. Ashurst, the team had a special carriage to convey them to their destination, and they arrived at Brad- ford at 2.30. Here they were met by Mr. J. Whittle (the captain of the "A" team), and after partaking of a slight luncheon were escorted to the Belle Yee Hotel, and quickly made ready to meet the foe. A slight breeze was blowing the length of the field, and Whittle winning the toes elected to play with the wind in his favour. About 5,000 specta- tors were present, and the ground was in good condition. Fawcett, for Manningham, kicked off, and Massey returned to touch. From the line out Richmond, from a pass by Birmingham, put in a good kick, and Kitchen followed to the line. Shortly afterwards the Warrington forwards worked the ball to the home goal line, and Fair Turner col- larcd Richmond with the ball on the line, a revisor shortly afterwarda resulting. From the kick out Barnes returned, and after a lot of give and take play three or four of the Warringtonians followed the ball up the field, Davies get- tug over the line and scoring the first try, from which Barnes kicked a nice goal amidst the cheers of the spectatars who had come from Bradford to witness the match. Fawcett kicked off, Barnes retaaning to centre. Holmes next got in a free kick from a high kick I by. Massey, but Barnes replied to this with interest. Barnes next got in a nice kick, and Whittle dribbled to the line. E. Holmes, however, saved, putting in a good run, but was collared by Massey and Littlewood. Holmes again got held and oy a strong run took play into the Warrington 25, where the bail remained for some time. A minor was the. result of a long kick by Richmond. Fair. Turner dropped Out, Richmond returning to Warrington quarters. Fawcett after the Warrington forwards had taken the ball to ceatr-s, put in a nice dodgy run. Lund stepping his progress. Ana trobus now showed up well, and Lund tried his best to get away, but passed in his own 25, play for some time being on the Warrington line. On the ball coming loose Barnes took a flying kick to touch, and the forwards werkkg well together, took play to centre, Fawcett kicking to touch. Good paseing among the War- rington backs took play to the borne line, but Richmond removed. Barnes kicked up the field, and for several minutes the Manningham lines were in danger until Francis Robinson relieved, Whittle from centre brae out with a beautiful dribble, and picking smartly up could easily have scored, but mast unselfishly Passed wide amongst the forwards. At this point of tha game W. Robinson was hurt and bad to retire for a short time. From a line out Noble obtained possession and succeeded in get- ting. over. Fawcett missing the goal. Fair. Turner kicked off, and Davies frustrated Biel:mend in his return. From the scrimmage Whittle saved well, and Massey Out in a good kick to touch. Birmingham now nearly got over, and at half-time the score was a goal and a minor for Wanington to a try and a minor for Manningham. Crossing over Frank Turner kicked off. and Fair Turner collared Toothill with the ball. It was thought that Manningham would equalize matters, but the Warringtonians playing well together stopped any score being made. Richmond from a pass by Birmingham failed to get hold, and the Warrington forwards got over the line, Littlewood dropping on the 'ball but the referee ordered a five yards scrimmage, Whittle next saved a rush, and by a long kick by Fawcett the ball fell into the hands of Speakman for the first time, and he kicked to touch. The Warrington forwards from the line ant worked the ball down the field, and E plain{ up nearly got over, but he was collared by Noble before he could transfer the ball to one of his side. Good Play •be- tween Fair Turner and Massey resulted in the latter , kicking to touch close to the line. The home forwards, however, removed to 25. Fawcett obtaining possession I ran up the field. In a lot of give and take play Fawcett I obtained a free kick and made a good drop at goal. From a scrimmage in the centre of the field a lot of others ensued, from one of which a dead ball was scored for Manningham. From the kick out the ball went to touch, Littlewo,cl and E. Dillon getting to the line. Again Littlewood got over, but the try was not allowed. From now until the call of time the play was of a give and take nature, and at the finish, attar seventy minutes' play, Warrington were declared the victors by one goal and two minors, to one try and two minors. All the Warrington men worked well together, Massey, Barnes Whittle, Antrobns, Davies, Fair Turner, and Littlewood the best. For Manningbam, Fawcett, Richmond, Holmes, and Birmingham strove hard to avert defeat.

The following aro. the teams :—Warrington—Back, W Speakman; threeqnarter backs, Land, Barnes, Massey ; half backs, Whittle and Antrobus ; forwards, Fair Turner, Frank Turner, Rigby, E. Dillon, Adamson, Littlewood, Davies, and Povey. Manningharn—Back, W Robinson ; threennarter backs, F Robinson, F Richmond, and W J Fawcett; hail backs, J Birmingham and E Holmes; for- wards, Tootbill, Barnett, Jewett, Clarkson,Noble, Rowlands, Mackay, Moxon, and Kitchen. Umpires, Messrs. Hartley and Barnes. Referee, Mr. Tomlinson (Cestleferd.) WARRINGTON v. WAKEFIELD TRINITY.

The great interest that was taken in the visit of the Yorkshire cupholders to Warrington was attested by the great attendance on the ground off Wilderspool Causeway on Tuesday afternoon. Fortunately the weather was all that could be desired: and the ground in excellent con- dition. The borne captain won the toes, and Booth, for Wake- field, kicked off with the wind slightly against him. Barnes, after a smart run, punted to the half.way flag, bat- Fallas returned to the Warrington quarter, and a smart re- turn left the play in the home half. The home team were placed on the defensive, and while in their quarter Wake- field were on the point of scoring, after a neat pass by Dunne to C6lley. A moment afterwards Dunne picked up and carried the ball over the line, and scored the first try for,Trinity. Whitley failed at goal. Ashton dropped out, and the Warringten forwards reached the centrefiag. Wake- field, however, threatened to invade the home quarter, when an effective return by Coop removed danger, and elicited a round of cheering. Dunne, after a short run, replied, and ' landed the ball into‘the Warrington ball. Play ensued for some minutes at centre flag, the home team offering a stubborn resistance to their opponents, the tackling of Speakman, Barnes, and Fair Turner being a conspicuous fea- ture. Wakefield continued to press, and J. Dawson, after a long kick by Colley, secured the ball, and was within a yard of striding over, when Barnes made a splendid tackle and ruined his opponent's chance. The Wakefield forwards then premed bard for a score and forced a touchdown. On the ball being brought out by Ashton it was returned to the home quarter, where Massey secured and made a splendid kick. Ashton obtained hold, but being collared he passed to Davies. The ball was transferred from hand to hand until the Wakefield lines were reached, where the home team granted a touchdown. By dint of hard play the Wakefield men again entered the home half, but relief was afforded by Antrobus, who, after a smart run, transferred to Massey, who finished a splendid piece of play by punting into the Wakefield quarter. Ash returned into the Warrington half, where the home team were again put on the defensive. After some strong play H. Dawson got over, but Whiteley's at- tempt at goal was a failure. On the ball being brought out, Ash returned. Barnes from his own quarter, afforded re- lief by punting to the centre, where a series of scrimmages ensued. Wakefield hact the balance of power in the for- ward division, and forced their opponents back upon their own touchline. Fair. Turner, Barnes, Jolley, Speakman, and Antrobus played a fine defensive game and their tack- , ling was sure. By some sterling play the ball was brought to the half, and a moment later Barnes gained possession, and with a splendid course before him he missed his chance by cilliding with the visitors' umpire, who teas promptly laid upon his back '„to the amusement of the spectators. Dillon came through with the ball at his feet, and Ashton and Fair Turner following up smartly, the ball reached the quarter, where Colley saved by falling on the ball. At half time the score stood at 2 tries and 2 minors for Wakefield, to 1 minor for Warrington. After the usual interval, Frank Turner kicked off for Warrington. liamshaw returned; but before Antrobus could retyrn he was tackled by Ross and Whitley+, who got into the Warrington half. gamey gave relief by punting into his opponents' quarters. Booth led through, and in a few momenta the ball fell into the bands of the backs, and some long exchanges took place between Ash and Coop. The Wakefield men again assailed the Warring.

Three men, name;l 51‘Growan, Guilpye, and Horan, were arrested near Loughrea on Wednesday night, charged with murdering a man named Baker, whose body was found covered with wounds recently. MIIIIDER OF A SwRETHEAEL—At Southampton, on Wed- nesday evening, a young man named George Early shot his sweetheart, Isabella Rose Fleming, aged nineteen, and then attempted suicide. Early called upon the girl, who lived with her parents. They were alone in the kitchen, and the girl's mother heard her daughter scream and then cry out, "Oh mother, he has shot me." Two reports of a pistol were beard quickly following each other' and on Mrs. Fleming going into the kitchen she found her daughter bleeding from a wound in the breast and Early bleeiling from a wound in the mouth. The girl died almost Immo. diately. Early was removed to the inftrmary. Tim Cnswa MURDER.—The Crewe magistrates yvere en- gaged on Thursday for several hours investigating the charges preferred against the young man Bevin of murder- ing his aunt, Mrs. Griffiths, and attempting to murder his cousin, Mary Jones, a girl nine years of age. Evidence was given regarding the finding in her own house of Mrs. Grif- fiths's body by her husband on his return Irons work, and some witnesses were called who stated that they saw Sevin near the house shortly before the crime was discovered. His arrest and the replies he made to certain ‘. leading '' interro- gatories put by police officers to him were also related, and a further remand for a week was taken.

NOTES BY THE WAY.

We understand that eighteen Clubs have entered for the junior competition inaugurated by the Warrington Football Club, so that there is every prospect of the competi- tion answering the purpose for which it was started, namely, encouraging the game amongst the yonnger generation. The draw, ne understand, wan to take place .at night, and the results of it will probably be known to most of those concerned bv the time this note reaches the eye of the public. The proceeds of the competition, it may be men- tioned, will go in aid of charities, We believe that Warren is again about to try his hand the Warrington team, and it is to Se hoped that he will this time be more fortunate than formerly with regard to in- juries. A more gentlemanly player does not 'rake part in football.

Warrington did not come out of their encountee with the Yorkshire cup holders in as brilliant a fashion as Weir ad- mirers had hoped for. Lately, from one c Anse or another, they have had a good daal of " chopping and changing" in their team, and this, as every one knaws is not favourable to that organisation and unity of action, which are neceoeary to first-class play, and which Warricgton bad worked up to a pretty high state of perfection. There was a notice• able contrast in the style of play of the two teams. The passing of the Yorkshiremen, especiaNy from the so...rim- mages, was systematic, and their backs- made a point of getting rid of the ball, wherever possible, either by kicking or passing before being collared. As a consequence there was not so many inetances of brilliant individual play, 'eit the whole team worked to each other's hands in a splendidly organised manner. On the other hand, although the War- rington men individually played a strenuous game, they did not by any means work so well together as their opponenee did, or indeed, as they generally do themselves. The half- backs, in particular, instead of passing quickly, but with. precision, to•those behind; showed an undue partiality for trying to do something, sensational on their own account; Judging by appearances the Warrington three-quarters and full back were in no way inferior to their opposites, but while the latter were afforded every opportunity of doing good work for their side, the - former had comparatively little to do, at all events in the way of aggressive play. • There has been quite a carnival of football over the Easter. holidays, nearly all the MOM famous clubs of Lancashire, Yorkshire, and Westmoreland' having had several engage- ments to meet. Among the-Westmereland Clubs the Keedal Hornets have been very busy, and as usual have given a • good account of themselves. On Friday they met Moseley on their ground and sent them back defeated to the tune of two goals, one try, and three minors, to two minors. On Saturday the Hornets run up a score against Birch of one goal, three tries, and.seven minors tonothing. On Saturday Salford met the Barrow men on the ground of the latter, and came away victorious, baying notched two goals, one try, and five minors, to one try and three miners. On Monday,. however, Barrow were more fortunate on ifleeting Manning- ham, with whom they drew a game, the score being Barrow four minors, Manningbamtwo minors. Asnull, on Seim- day, upheld their reputation as the West Lancashire cup- holders, as they manageetto draw with the famous York- shire team, Leeds Parish Church, the score being Leads, one goal and three minors, to Aspnll one goal and one minor. The following team has been chosen to represent West Lancashire in the match with Westmorland, at Widnes, on Thursday, the 21st lust. :—West Lancashire : G. Pilking- ton (Asprill), back Davies. (Runcorn), Barnes, and J. Jolley (Warrington), thrge-quarter • backs ; IL, Hughes I (Runcorn): ad D. Hume (Aspull), half-backs ; R. Wil- cock (Liverpool Wanderers), W. R. Broady (Runcorn), L. H. Smith (Widnes), F. Touter (Warrington), J. Whittle (Wigan), J. Pyke and W. Parr (St. Helens Recreation), J. Monks (Wigan), and J. Holmes (Litherland), forwards. First Reserve: J: Pilkington (St. Helens Recreation), three-quarter back E. Kiddie (Widnes), forward. Referee : Mr. G. Rowland Kick oft at six o'clock.

div.head: THELWALL.
div.p: THELWALL.

The annual vestry rneeting was held on Monday In the schoolroom at 7 p.m. Mr. Norman Taylor and Mr. Thomas Cook were elected churchwardens, Mr. A. Roebuck and Mr. henry Beckett, eideemen, and Mr. Henry Bleokly and Mr. B. A. Naylor the lay delegates.

div.head: STRETTON.
div.p: STRETTON.

The annual vestry meetin74-t-h-ok-place at twelve o'clock on Easter Monday. in the schoolroom, the Rev Canon Dodd, vicar of the parish, occupying the chair. The churchwar- dens, Mr. John Edmund Davies, of Broom Cottage Apple- ton, and Mr. R. Hi Kerr, of Spark Hall, Stretton, submitted their accounts, from which it appeared that the total e:zpen- diture -amounted to £45 51 9ti, and the receipts from volun- tary subahriptions, including £5 from the offertory, to £47 1284 d, leaving a balance in hand of £2 63 7d. Yo'..;es of thanks were passed to the churchwardens for their services, and the same gentlemen were re-ele.lted for the ensuinE,, year. Mr. T. Dichtield was reelected eidesman. HOLY TRINITY RUNCORN.

• The annual vestry was held in the Ohurch,•on Monday night under the presidency of the Vicar, the Rev. W. Pres- ton about a -dozes persons were present, Mr. W. Fisher, the Vicars Warden, presented the accounts which showed that during the year the income had bsen £B4 183 80,, and the expenditure £66 3s Oid leaving a deficit of .£9l; 4s 4d. The income for 1885. was £TS 18s 2. The accounts having been audited, were passed on the motion of Mr. E. Timmins oeconded by.afr.Hankinson.—ln a brief speech the vicar reviewed the work of the past year, and remarked that he was thankful, things, both in the parish and amongst tiro aongregation, were satisfactory. He mentioned that the sum of .d3BO bad been received in contribution from persons outside the parish towards the enclosure of the land adjoin- ing the Church. He spoke in terms of praise of thelaboars of the Wardens and re-elected Mr. Fisher as Vicar's Warden. On the proposition of Mr. Fisher seconded by Mr, Hankin- son, Mr. John Buckley was re-appointed peoples Warden Messrs W Hankinson, J Foulkes, H. Savage, and. 14 Kilcross were appointed sidemen, whilst Messrs E Timmins and 31 H Salkild were elected members of the Church Council.. Messrs W\ Fisher and W liankinson .were: selected as ruri, decanal representatives. On the proposal of the Vino sec- ondedby Mr. Fisher, and supported by Mr. W Leathwood a cordial vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Timmins for his generosity in providing the Church with a new heating apperatus.• The choir, the choirmaster (Mr. Ainsworth); and tbnorganist (Mr. Hatton) were heartily thanked for their past services. , FAIttiWOHTH PARISH CERYRCH.

The annual meeting of tips parishioners was held in St. Luke's Church, on Thursday afternoon. The Rev. George Bonds (vicar) presided. The accounts, which showed a balance of XS Is Oki owing to thq trasurer, wore unani- raonely passed. The vicar again selected Mr. Peter Long- ton as his warden, and the remaining wardens were appointed as follows :7Cuerdlev, Mr. Matthew Taylor; Bold, Mr. Baker; Crouton, Mr. Peter Glover. The sues- men were re-elected, with the addi6oh of Mere. Chad- wick, Carlisle, and Brown.—The Vimr remasked that the sum of 111,200 lead been promised towards the restoration of 1 the church, and he thought they aught to signalise the- jubilee of the Queen's reign by carrying out the work. He had written to the Duke of Westminster with regard to the subject, but the Duke had so much to do, and besides was so poor—he believed he had £3,000 day—that nothing was. obtained front him. He intimated that he would call a meeting of the Church Council to consider how the restora. Clan should be carried out. Alluding to the question of the proprietorship of pews, the Vicar said another difficulty had arisen. As regarded the bottom of the church, there was.no proprietorship, hoc in the galdery, where the case had oc- carredabere were documents relating to the purchase and letting of pews. A gentlemen had claimed spew, whith another gentleman had.sat in for some considerable time, on the ground that it had been lei him by a lady. By desire of the churchwardens, he (the vi9ar) was going to sae the Bishop's secretary on. the; subject, and probably it would be satisfactorily settled.—There was no other business of interest__ .

------ FRODSTIAX PARISH CHURCH. The Easter vestry was held in the Kingsley Chapel at the Parish Church on Monday morning. The Rev. ii. B. Blogg presided, and there was a good attendance of parishioners. The accounts of the churchwardens showed that the income for the year amounted to £2TB Ts 10d, including offertories £177 2s 6d, and collections for charities 159 73 7d. The expenditure amoented to 24 8s 2d, thas leaving a balance In band of £43 Ws 84. The accounts were passed.—Mr. A. Thomas, J.P. having expressed a wish not to again be ap. pointed as vicar's warden, the Chairman elected Mr. C. H. Linaker in his stead. Messrs Thomas Davies, George Gleave, R. Bate, and A. E. Pollard were elected sidesmen, and Messrs J. Robinson and H. Tilly were appointed lay representatives —During a discussion as to the trusteeship of the Bible Class Band, which the vicar handed ovor as a parish trust. it was reported that Mr. C. Reynolds had con- tributed £24 3s 94 to the funds of the rand as a jubilee offering, and that gentleman was thanked for his generosity. —Mr. G. H. Denby was also thanked for his services to the 'baud during the year. The committee appointed to inquire

Into the objects and constitution of the organ trust presented a lengthy report, which they concluded by stating I. That the land belonging to the trust consists of 15a. lr. 14p. statute measure, producing& rent of £3O par annum. I—II. That the object of the trust is for the purpose of 'paying the organist of the Parish Church and keeping the I organ in repair.—111. That the number of the Trustees is five.-IV. That four of the trustees are appointed by the ' freeholders of the parish. and that the inner warden for the time being in a Trustee by virtue of bin office.—V. That the Trustees have the right of appointing and dismissing the organist." It was resolved unanimously that the report be adopted and entered on the minutes.—The Church Tower IRestoration Committee reported that the work bad been • completed. The' bells had been re-hung, and the framing 'Fad been constructed with a view to receiving two addi- tional balls to complete the octave. A very valuable clock, , manufactured by Messrs Joyce and Co., of Whitchtirch, had been presented to tbe church by' the Misses Ashley, and ' bad been so4arranged that chimes ceuld be added when the necessary funds were forthcoming'. The committee thought, that when all liabilitierwere discharged, they would have a balance in hand of at least N.so'. This report was also adcpted.—At a subselhent meting of the freeholders Messrs W. Hayes, J. Aschton, Charles Reynolds, are Alfred Thomas were appointed trustees of the "(Veen Lot." WARGRAFE CHURCH. The parishlemers of this-church held their annual vestry meeting on Tuesday afteraoon, when,the Rev. Canon Whit- ley, M.A., rector, who prezided, was supported by Messrs j William Thompson, Btarkia, H Thompson, Tootall, James I Davies, e7e. After the minutes of the, last annual meting ; had been confirmed, the amounts mere considered. The wardens' accounts showed a balance of £2 48 7d in hand; ' and the Organ Fund balance sheet, read by Mr William Thompson, ehowed that the expeameo in connection with the new orgeei and the cost of-tbe new desks for the school,- 'in all, a total ()reheat £BOO, bad been &hayed. 'The par- lishioners present expressed that they were very highly ; gratified that se much had been raised, and so great a debt cleared off. The rector again nominated Mr. William 'I Thompson as bite-Warden, and Mr. T. Molvnews was re- appointed parishioners' warden. Messrs William Thonap- son. junior, Tootall;. Starkie, Catherall, Moss, Sweetlove. Haeeldine, Purnell, and Cave were re-elected sidesmen. The salaries of the church. officers (organist and choirmaster) were fixed the same as last yea and the vestry awarded a gratuity of £lO to the choir for their services. Mr. Wm. Thompson, senior, and Mr. Tootall'were re-elected lay re- presentatives to the Rirri-Decanal Conference ;. and a vol- untary church rate of al in the mime as last year,. arhen about £l6 were realised, was decided upon. During the evening it was stated that there was a prospect of farther I improvements in the church during tile ensuing year.. The I meeting was thoroughly-harmonious,

Dr. Oqieeffe, as retuning officer, reported that the 11Ye retiring members, Messrs. Goesege, Haskell, Sadler, Hand kr, and Carey, bad been returned without a contest. He thought this fact showed that the ratepayers of Widnes and the pelple generally reposed that confidence in those gentle- men which their work during the past three years deeorved hear)—and he was quite note that as they had given the ratepayers the benefit of their great experience on the Hoard in important matters of business, it would have teen a great loss to the ratepayers to have lost the services-of any, of tlaerm. GAS AND WATER COMAE:M.

The Engineer reported to this committee that Dr. Camp- bell Brown had during the past month, analysed samples of Stock's well and/tetherley waters, and declare l both to be of excellent quality for domestic use. A waste water meter bad been fixed at the bottom of Pubhonse-lane for ehecking the waste of the north 'east portion of' the township, in- cluding- Appleton,. Halton-view, Crow, Wood, Warrington- road, and Llllo4ol* districts, and is designated Appleton district. The number of houses and shops supplied with water was 741 i or about 3.700 inhabitants. Tho total con- sumption per bead per day was 14 gallows, 9 of Which was shown to be waste. There were now four waste water meters at work, ,the total population under the system being 18,4,16:, A leeter had been received fromthe Local Govern- ment Board stating that inquiries were being Made as to the pollution of Netherley Brook: It Vi9t9 recommended that Messrs. .L Muspratt and Son, and Mr. A,Farrell,Lugsdale- lane, be prosecuted for using water without having obtained permission, and. Messrs. Potts and Appleton for damaging water pipes and taps, and for wasting water. Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Preecot Union, wrote and informed the committee that the Assessment Committee had reduced the rateable value-of the Gas Werke from £3.102 to £2,505, and of the Water Works from £7,698 to 28,743.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. 8.. Brown, seconded by Mr. Taylor, the former gentleman remarking that the sav- ing effected by the waste water meters had far exceeded the anticipationa.of the committee.

The Medical Officer (Dr. Cooper) presented his report for March- in otebtoh aniongst other things be said I an sorry, to have to report two cases of typhoid fever, one in Thorp street and the second in a milk house in Rose-street ; in the latter ease we immediately cut off MI eammtanteition. between the shop where the milk is sold and the house, by nailing up the door and pasting it round with paper. , We. also prohibite I any communication between the person taking charge of the milk and the fever patient. WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board. was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Black. hurst, J. Houghton W. Houghton, Brown, Isher- wood, Clark, Ratcliffe, Eckersley, Wright, Harri- son; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and, S. Sutton (assistant clerk).

div.head: SCHOOLS COMHITTEH.
div.p: SCHOOLS COMHITTEH.

The minutes of this committee stated that the committee desired to tender to Mr. W. Houghton a vote of thanks for his Easter present to the children of a box pf oranges. ,The medical officer repo-ted the general health of the children to be excellent.—On the motion of Mr, J. HownitTow, seconded by Mr. RATCLIFFE, the minutes were confirmed.

div.head: SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE.

The School Nees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 49 cases. 38 of which were old, and 11 new cases. —On the motion of Mr. Buicimunsr, seconded by Mr. RATCLIFFE, the minutes were confirmed.

div.head: HOUSE COMMITTEE.
div.p: HOUSE COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of this Committee it was reportel that in accordance with the Board's resolution of the 16:h March Mr. Harbourne took over the charge of the house on Satur- day, the 26th inst. Mr. and Mrs. Mackey left the house on Tuesday, the 28th inst. Since then Mr. Harbeurne had had uninterrupted charge of the houee. The committee consider the management of the establishment to be satis- factory. At the subsequent meeting of this committee it was reported that Mr. Mackey had produced his account books made up to the end of the quartet ready for the audi- tor's examination. The farm account book showed a profit equal to £lB 2s 8d for the half year.—On,ltbe motion of Mr. Snows, seconded by Mr. ISHERWOOD, the minutes were passed.

VOTES OF THANKS. Mr. BrAcinttrusT said that all that was the last meeting of the year for which the chairman had been elected, he bad much pleasure in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Roberta for the very satisfactory manner in which he had conducted the business of the Board during the last twelve months. (Hear, bear.—Mr. HARRISON, in seconding the proposal, referrec4 to the courtesy, impartiality, dignity, firmness, and tact which had distinguished the conduct of the chairman during his last year of office.—The proposal was supported by Mr. W. Houghton, Mr. Brown, and Mr. Ratcliffe.—The CLERK, in putting the proposal to the meetiwg, mentioned that Mr: Greening called upon hint a week ago, and said ;hat in con- sequence of indisposition be was going to Windermere, but he expressly desired to join in the vote of thanks to the chairman.—The vote was then accorded by acclamation, and the CHAIRMAN suitably responded.—Mr. RATCLIFFE next moved, in complimentary terms, a vote of thanks to Mr. Balharry, the sewior vice-chairman. He mentioned that Mr. Balharry presided over their Newton Relief Com- mittee, and the relief in the Newton district was dispensed in a manner which would compare favourably with any other district.—Mr. WRIGHT seconded the proposal, which was supported by the Chairman and unanimously agreed to.—Mr. HARRISON, in moving a vote of thanks to the junior vice-chairman, Mr. Brown, referred to the indefatigable services rendered by that gentleman to the Board as chair- man of the House Committee.—Mr. IsnErtwoon seconded this proposal, which, after having ybeen supported by Mr. W. Honotri.ox and the CHAIRMAN, Was cordially passed, and Mr. BROWN briefly responded. The relief cases were then proceeded with.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WARRINGTON. _ _
div.p: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WARRINGTON. _ _

On Wednesday evening a meeting of Conserva- tives was held at the Conservative Club, Sankey- street, to support the coercive Irish legislation of the Government. Captain Reynolds presided, and there was a good attendance, amongst those present being Aldermen Sutton, Webster, and Harrison, the Rev:E. C. E. Carelton, Councillors T. Jolley, J. Pier- point, and Francomb, Major Litton, Captain Nichol- son, Mr. J. W. Burgess (Liverpool), Mr. Croston (Manchester), and Mr. Hampson (secretary of the Conservative Association). Letters regretting in- ability to be present had been received from Mr. W. Beamont, Mr. Bleckly, and other gentlemen. Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P. for the borough, who had been announced to speak, was prevented by Parliamentary duties from being present.—The CHAIRMAN, in opening the meeting, remarked, that the measure which they had Met to support hadnow

I passed the first reading not by a nariOw majority, but by a majority of 108. (Cheers.) The Irish question was one that had taken up far too much time in Parliament, with the consequence that other matters were not receiving an adequate share of attention. They must determinedly show that it was the opinion of the country that this should not continue, and that the continual ob- struction of Parliamentary business should cease. They in Warrington could help by sending a resolu- tion to the Conservative leaders approving of the , bill now before Parliament. (Cheers.) He had hoped that the member for Warrington would have , been present, but Sir Gilbert Greenall had gone to London to be ready at the call of duty. Whenever he was wanted at a division Sir Gilbert was there, and they would agree with him that Sir Gilbert was made of the right kind of stuff. (Cheers.) The time and attention he had given to his Parliamen- tary duties was pr99f 9f that, Ile hoped that tho resolution that would be nut Wert them would be carried with enthusiasm, (Cheers.)—Mr. W. J. Bun- GESS proposed the following resolution :—" It being the opinion of this meeting that a state of or- ganised intimidation and outrage exists in Ireland, the object of which is to effect the separation of that country from the United Kingdom, and that in the event of the Parnellite conspirators, with the assistance of the Gladstone Separatists., being successful, the interests and safety of our empire would be greatly endangered, this meeting desires to express its entire ligreement and sympathy with the Government tn its legisla- tive proposals for the just admint'stration of the law, and for the protection of Ute and property in Ireland, believing that by tht's means alone justice to the loyal Irish and safety to the United Kingdom can be maintained." The Government, he said were perfectly willing tO grant many reforms to Ireland, and had brought 'forward an Irish Land Bill, Their coercive proposals were, such as no law-abiding citizen could object to, because they aimed at putl• thig.down the lawless conspiracy in Ireland against the liberty, the property, and the lives of those who would not join the National League. Mr. Gladstone had allied himself with Mr. Parnell in obstructing business in the House of Commons, and Mr. Parnell and his friends had determined to try and show the people of the United Kingdom that it was impos- sible for England to rule Ireland by an Imperial Parliament, after the people of this country had declared that Ireland should be so ruled. He thought that Mr. Parnell would not be prepared to overrule the decision of the people. ef England. (Cheers.)—Mr. APPLETON 'seconded the resolution, and remarksd that Mr. Gladstone was in league with a set of 'rebels and assassins.— Mr. PETER NAYLOR'S 'wdliing man, supported the resolution,which was cried with unanimity.—Mr. CROSTON (Manchester) then gave an address on the present political sittnitima. We were now face to face with a great crisis,andwithregardto it the meeting that night had given its opinion in an unmistak- able manner. At the last election Mr. Gladstone found himself in the cold shade of opposition, and he was now 'anxious to get back to office, and he and his agents were seeking to discredit the Go- I vernment in power. He denied that the legislative I proposals for Irish Government were coercive, and remarked that the Bill was for the emancipation of Ireland, for the freedom of Irishmen from the gall- ing tyranny, and the oppression of the treasonable land league. The condition of things in Ireland was a stain upon the very name of humanity, and in the interests of Irishmen, and of civilisation, the Government was bound to put a stop to it. The Government looked to the country to justify them in their action, and they had done their duty by paising the resolution.—Mr. R. W. FRANComB moved That the best thanks of the meeting are due and are hereby respectfully tendered to our member, Sir Gilbert Greenall, hart., for the close attention he has given to his Parliamentary duties during the recent protracted' sittings of the House of Com- mons, caused by the persistent obstruction to all legislation by the Parnell-Gladstone party."—The resolution was seconded by CAPTAIN NlcHonsoN, and 'carried, after which the meeting terminated.

ABOUT A SELF-IMPOBTANT ,Orm.—Not long ago a mis- cellaneous party of visitors was being shown over Chats- worth. One of them, a stout over-dressed lady, feeling herself socially considerably above her fellow-sightseers, determined that they should be duly impressed with this fact. So after a time she turned to the house- keeper who was conducting the party, and said, "And how is the Duke? He wasn't very well when I saw him last." "His Grace has a slight cold," replied the housekeeper, "but otherwise is in the best of health." After allowing the company sufficient time to recover from the first feeling of awe which naturally fell upon them on discovering that she was so well acquainted, the lady resumed, "And how is the dear Duchess." "The duchess, madam, has been dead the last thirty years !"
