Srattero to et ttittor. THE INCREASE OF RATES IN WARRINGTON. Sir —ln last aturday's Examiner," I notice you prom- ise to refer next Saturday to the abov3 question, and invite your readers also to have their say on this subject. Well, the mischief is done, bat still we can grumble, and aeon the face of it we ratepayers are having to pay a heavy bill and getting no explanation of the increase, it is time the Corpor- ation should know that we are not satisfied. I have read carefully the reports of the Council Meeting of last Tues- day, and I only intend to refer te what is reported, though one has heard plenty of gossip on the question since. In the first place, I notice that this year the Council have arranged for the Committees to give their estimated expen- diture for 12 months, instead of six, and have on that levied rates for 12 months and not nix, though payable in two in- stalments. This may be a wise and economical plan or it may possibly be done to hide a large deficiency by spread- ing it over twelve instead of six months. But, whatever the reason, the rates are to be. during the ensuing twelve menthe 4d in the £ higher than last year. In the present depressed times this comes heavy on some, If not all of us, and one naturally expects some explanation. I have searched through the reports of the Council Meeting in vain for such. It is. true that Aldermen Holmes and Burgess, on being questioned about the Sanitary Committee estimates, admitted, that this committee had overspent their borrowing powers by £l,OOO, but Alderman Burgess in reply to the Mayor said this £l,OOO was included in ' their estimate for the year, which is £3OO leas than last year, so the 4d extra is not needed there. Where then comes the necessity for the extra money? Have we not a right to know these things? Evidently our representatives in the Council think not, or they surely woula have given some explana- tion last Tuesday. All we are told is that a summary of the estimates shows a requirement of £2B 232 this year, against £24,809 last year, an increase of £3400. Now, Mr. Editor, I submit this is not a proper treatment. Those who find the money have a right to know how and why it is used, and one would have thought that the time and opportunity for such explanation, was last Tuesday evening, when the "Budget "was passed. Nearly all our Town Councillors when they Leek election, tell us their determination to go in for economy. 'Where were they all last Tuesday? Were they satished with the mere moving the adoption of the minutes by the several chairmen of Committees? Or bad they further information which is not vouchsafed to the public? In either case I fancy their constituents will hard- ly be satisfied with their conduct; they certainly won't if they are of the same mind as yours truly A RATEPAYER.

COERCION v. JUSTICE TO IRELAND. Sir,—l find it very difficult to understand the presen state of quietness and apparent apathy of my fellow-conn- trymen in this district at a time when the very life and liberty are in danger of being crush d out of our kindred in our native land. Are we to wait to be dragged along by the wheels of the English political car before we can show ourselves folly alive to the great importance and bearing this most drastic of repressive measures will have upon the future progress of our country? Stripped of its most loathsome garment, it reveals itself as one of the most diabolical schemes that human ingenuity could invent. Shades of Emmett and Grattan, though their voice is for ever silent, their cause still lives. Wherever the seas roll and the glorious sun shines, the song is sung and the aspirations expressed lav thousands of Ireland's eons upon behalf of their fatherland. Crime may de present in many parts of Ireland at the present time, and the Government of the day may find it very difficult to grapple with it; but when we know that 90 per cent of the crime is agrarian,the root of which is not of recent production, tut the growth of centuries et robbery and maladministration, it seems a strange teethed to cause the law to be respected by repeatedly resort- ing to penal enactments to protect the unscruplous rapacity of rack-renting landlords and land grabbers. Can we wonder at the social disorder complained of when we see a noble race of people driven back from the paths of ; I was almost saying cut off from all connections with the outer world—driven back upon the mountains and morasses of his native land by strangers, while the beasts of the field roam the fertile plains and valleys where man should have his homestead. I have been in my day a keen observer of man and his surrounding. and nowhere have I fonnfi such helpless submission to their lot as I fonnd in the breasts of the peasantry of the poorer districts of Ireland. But, sir, beneath that quiet submission to fat., there burns a soul- born love and aspiration for the time to come when his wrongs shall be redressed; when his wild dirge of lamen- tation shall be turned into a song of joy ; when nature shall yield to him freely what she now deals out to him with a stinted hand. Can anyone wonder that he may give way to fits of piseions, and seek revenge upon those be deems the cause of his present miserable condition? The Irish peasant has been the shuttlecock of English politics or ages. Statesmen have grown old in the service of the Crown. Most of them bays commenced their career 1 in atte.mpting to grapple with the Irish question, and tw far the larger number have admitted that coercion has always failed in fulfilling the objects for which it was intended. Coercion has driven millions of Ireland's children across the seas. No one clings with greater tenacity to his native land than tile Irishman. No one who has stood upon the quays of Cork or Liverpool can fail to have been touched with the scere of tender partings of youth and old age, or with the expressions of deep love and invocation of blessings that go forth for the welfare of the departing friends and relations. It is a sight not soon to be forgotten. The Irish peasant leaves behind him a misgoverned country in which he finds it impossible any longer to live, sorrowing. relations, and generally a broken op homestead robbed of its bread- winner. Can he be blamed if he carries with him in exile bitter recollections, which often bear very detrimentally upon the interest of England? In this.country the Irishman has become in the full en- joyment of the franchise an important factor in the elec- tions. At no period did duty ever call upon them with stronger claims than at the present time to make that power felt. As peaceful citizens, let them ask justice at the hands of our rulers. All lawful pressure we can bring to bear in the form of petition or demonstration will support the hands of the aged chief who stands now in the breach doing" battle even unto death for our cause. Shall we, then' stand idly by while the roar of battle is heard around us? Let our voice be heard protesting against this last but most drastic of all the coercion laws that has ever been put into operation to attempt to rule a subject nation. Future generations will Wok back upon our present actions; let not our voice be silent, or our pen be still, in the coming great struggle. T. F.

THE INFLUENCE OF MACHINERY ON THE PROSPERITY OF THE PEOPLE. Sir,—l met apologise for asking for a little more of your Vane. The question as to the sum of human happiness is air important one, and can be looked at from myriad points of view. I should like to bring out one or two of these Points. In the Words of the 66 Spectator," "the strife be- tween capital and labour rises black and menacing above the pear horizon," and as one of the labour party I am anxious about the "machine." To Mr. Gandy I would say with all respect he is not qualified to give even an opinion upon se important a question. His training, and everyday surroundings terma it; and it needs but his last letter as proof that hie reading has been "superficial." Of Mr. Morris I do not saw the same; but I think even he will allow that his everyday life during the last thirty years has left him little tioarator wide and general reading. While not pretending. that the " " is either close upon us, or likely to be for some days, I still hope to be allowed to do my little towards bridging ever the gulf that yawns between the Classes and the masses. "The condition of the people has been happier since the introduc- tion of machinery than it ever was before"; so says Mr. Ciandy. I deny it in tote. If Mr. Gandy will allow that the

party—all for what? Simply this, to:enable the Tories to keep out of office the man they have ever bated and dreaded. I for one refuse to accept any man as a Liberal who votes or supports coercion. Let him stand forth for what he is, and presume not to call himself a "Real Unionist" when his real title is" Coercioniat." Now then what is it these coercioniets want? The "in- tegrity of the empire maintained," say they. Well, how is it to be maintained? Does past history tbrow any light on this question? Surely it does. John Bright, speaking at Rochdale, December 23rd, 1867, said—"l entirely disagree with those who, when any crisis or trouble arises, say that you mast first of all preserve order, you must assert the supremacy of the Government, and then consider the grievances that are complained of. Generally, after having asserted the supremacy of the law, and having made what they call peace under the terrors of the law, the grievances are forgotten, and there is no consideration of them. This has been the case in Ireland for two hundred years. The great preservers there have been the gibbet and the gal- lows." Coercionists need not be afraid of their able ally, John Bright. The quotations I give are from speeches de- livered by the People's Tribune when he was in his prime, and when he said, speaking of Home Rule—" Suppose it were possible for these men, with their intellects, with their far-reaching vision, to examine the question thoroughly, and to say /or once, whether this leads to office, and to the miserable notoriety that men call fame, which springs from office, or not, if it be possible we will act with loyalty to the Sovereign and justice to the people; and if it be pos- sible, we will make Ireland a strength and not a weakness to the British Empire."—Speech in the House of Commons, February 17, 1866. Again, he said—" We who ask Parlia- ment, in dealing with Ireland, to deal with it upon the unchangeable principles of justice, are the friends,of the people, and the really loyal advisers and supporters of the throne." How comes it that an able advocate of a people's cause should tarn round On the above sentiments, forswear his own teachings,- and expect a party to follow hint? Speaking in the House of Commons, August 25, 1848, Mr. Bright said—" To-day anything that can be effectual must be infinitely less dangerous than to do nothing." What the Liberal patty propose to do is, and here comes., the bitter pill for the Tories, to carry out to its logical con, clneions the recent People's Representation Bill. Me.- Gladstone's position is clear and definite. When the people demand a thing they must have it, and all the Tory-Whig-I Radical-coercioniste-for-ever-and-ever must be brushed out ' of the way. ;retard sneaks through her representatives, and she cadet be listened to. Coercionists would, perhaps, like another quotation from John Bright. Here it is:— "They (theteaints hfErigland and Scotland) are much more powerful than the tenants Are there, because you, act- ing alone, have to act upon a great and powerful body in London. If you. had a Parliament in College Green, &ea" the tenantry of Irelamt, with the present feeling in Irelant, would be able to force that Parliament to any measure ot, justice they nulled; but as you have to deal with a great Parliament sitting in London, all the clamour you make, or the demands you .nay urge from this side of the Channel, come with a feeble effect, specially as it can only be repre- sented by about one hundred members, and of these it un- fortunately happens that a considerable number are not willing to support the demands that are made. . . . It is one et the most difficult things in the world for fifty men acting among six hundred men some hundreds of miles from those whem they represent, to work up any questions which may be against the prejudices and sympathies of the six hundred among whom they are acting."—Speech in reply to a deputation from . the Cork Farmers' Club, " Time)," November 1. 1886. I hope our Liberal Coercionis's friends have been at the trouble to study the -Report of the Cowper Land Commis- sion. I know the Tories would think it wasted time. At p. 223; Mr. Maccrtinrey a Tory Orangeman is asked—" You say there are some landlords who have not given judicial rents "? "There always are hard landlords who raise the rents as long as they can. That was the cause of the agita- tion in Ireland." Now. I ask Coercionist, or any Tory, What can be thought of a man like this, who can put his finger on Ireland's trouble and still by his actions seek to perpetuate it? tOut upon such double-facod Unionists, they are traitors to their country, and to their fellOvr men, and if the men of England allow them to go on they will bring their country to disgrace and ruin. The Commission to which I hive referred included a tenant farmer Mr. Knipe, who seems to be well able to grasp the situation. He says, —"The landlords, with a few honourable exceptions, have failed to meet by prompt *reductions of rent the serious fall in prices, or to recognize the serious losses to their tenants, and to this may be attribeted the combination and the re- sistance to eviction which has taken place and is likely to happen." If Coercionist knows anything cf either English or Irish history. be knows that mince 1832 we have been mainly en- gaged in repealing bad laws. According to • Baron Penne- ' father, "The entire landlord and tenant code goes to give Increased facilities to the landlord. It never entered the head of the Legislature to make provision for the tenant; and all these enactments, are invasions of the common law." I wish the Coercionists to study these points. They are the cause of the present ill-feeling betwixt the two nations. Why was Mr. Gladstone supported by the nation in his en- deavours to pass his Land Bill? Because you could not trust the Irish landlord to deal with his Irish tenants. Can you trust them today? Surely not; the leopard has not changed his spots, nor is likely to do. The time is near at band when tha same will be said of the English landlord. After the Lin act of 1870 was passed landlords forced leases lon their tenants upon the most unjust terms. Now, we are to have 3 special measure for breaking these forced contracts land we are to have a leaseholders' Bill. Your readers will remember, if Coercionists have forgotten, the most plain- tive speeces that were made about "Freedom of Contract" by the Tories. What about that now? Like everything else the Tories touch, they were only intended as" crutches" to be thrown away when they had served their day. It is safe to prophecy that the Liberal Coerctoniete wll be served the same as soon as the Tories think they have the game in their own hand. Like the Brad laugh incident, the Closure incident, and numberless other incidents, each one serve, as the last straw, to the drowning Tory party; they clutch at them with all the eagerness of a drowning man, and what is it for? To press-ye the a' Integrity of the Empire." To preserve something that doesn't exist, never aid exist, and never will, so long as bonds of iron ard forged by a grasping and selfish party. I believe there are working-mien, fools enough to think they are patriotic by keeping la" a Tory Government. They are blind, and cannot see they are helping the land grabbing class to stave off the greatest of all questions, viz., the Land Question, and so are fighting the landlords' battle. UNIONIST.

div.p: 19th century has ushered in diseases unknown to our fore- j fathers, has caused lunatic asylums to increase in numbers, ' has brought poverty in its bitterest aspect, face to face with luxury in its most effeminate form, then we shall be more in accord with each other. "Suppose the Messrs. Rylands were to close their works, where would the men be likely to get employment?" Sir, I am surprised at so simple a ques- tion. I thought we were dealing with principles. But, however, let us sumpose such an awfal calamity did occur, what then? Would the Messrs. Rylands commence eating their gold? If so, how long would it last? When their gold was done, the workman would still have his muscles. Now let me put another question—Suppose all the work- people of Warrington cease purchasing from Warrington tradesmen, where would the Warrington tradesmen be likely to find their customers? I can fancy Mr. Gandy getting the bit between his teeth at reading this, and muttering " what silly stuff 'Colin 'does but write." Mr. Gandy again shows his inability to deal with this question in his references to my example of the shoe trade. He says "A very large portion of the goods manufactured in this country is intended for export." Just so, but I fail to see that England is all the world. The I#bour question is International, and ia assuming proportions little dreamt of by easy-chair philosophers. Mr. Gandy seems to be greatly in love with Goldsmith. Does he fail ta see that the quotations he gives from poor old "Noll " are as ap- plicable to-day as ever they ware, and unless men put their whole souls into the work, will have to be doubly em- phasised. Mr. Gandy, in the last part of his letter, rather doubled me up by speaking of my "puny efforts to stem the on- ward march of mechanical development." I gather from this that he is of opinion that "things are beet as they are, and had better be let alone." If so, I differ from him im- mensely. I think that this development must be helped forward all that it possibly can ; that the potential powers of machinery should have all the scientific aid possible. I know, and could enumerate, scores of cases where machinery is gradually taking the place of manual labour; that is, man is becoming a mere machine-minder. More than this, I know men are gradually giving way to lads. Now then, who reaps the benefit? A Waterbury watch, worth 108 6d, made by machinery, displaces how many skilled men? A shoe made by machinery displaces how many skilled shoe- makers? A railway waggon made by machinery displaces how many skilled wheelwrights? And so we might go on. The first answer would be, as with the printing of the penny paper, the general public receives the benefit. Does the general public receive the profit? I have before me a list of millionares' wille during the past ten year. I won't touch it; but as its antithesis I may give this:—The monthly return of pauperism, just issued, shows that, whilst in February, 1884, there were 726.000 persons re- ceiving relief in England and Wales, the number in February last was 779,000. If this b satisfactory to Mr. Gandy it is net satisfactory to
COLIN CLOUT.

THE GOVERNMENT OF IRELAND. Sir,—Your correspondent signing himself "A Beal Unionist" may be excusA for the short-sightedness dis- played in his letter. Like all his party. he itrnores altogether the cause of present and past dissatisfaction in Ireland. and, looking only to the effect, argues from it that Irishmen are not qualified to govern their ,own land, and that they seek, only for self sh purposes, the disintegration of the empire. i will not insult the so-called Unionists by even hinting at their want of knowledge in Irish history. One could do it with more saft.ty and truthfulness if refer- ring to the I,,ries, and the Unimiets know thi-, to be so, but what is the position? Men who call tnemselves Liberals, or leaders in modes and methods in civilisation, are found allying themselves with the party justly characterised by John Bright as the "Stupid party." They are willing to go on for ever and ever, bolstering up an"organisedhypocrisy," satisfied, to act as crutches" to a lame and impotent . . _

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 16, 188, LATEST NEWS.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL The Eccles Co-operative Society proposes doubling the number of shares it holds in the Ship Canal, viz., from 100 to 200. At the quarterly meeting of the Little Hulton Co- operative Society, it was unanimously resolved to invest .£lOO with the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany. The society has now over 400 members, and a dividend of 3s 9d was declared. A requisition was presented to the Hyde Town Council on Monday night, from a number of local gentlemen, asking Pe Mayor to convene a meeting of leading ratepayers and traders for the purpose of taking into consideration the best means of assist- ing the directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Company in taising the capital necessary for the construction of the canal and works, it was resolved that a meeting should be held at an early date. At a meeting held on Wednesday evening at Stockport to consider the best means of assisting the Directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany to raise the capital necessary to commence the works, it was stated by Mr. C. Moseley, one of the members of the Board, that the amount at pre- sent subscribed in shares was .£1,900,000. The Directors, he said, had every hope that they would be in a position to ask the Prince of Wales to cut the first sod on the occasion of his forthcoming visit to Manchester. Speaking at a meeting at Bolton on Thursday afternoon Sir J. C.Lee said therhad promises which enabled him to say that the amount had been raised to £2,000,000. He had no doubt at all that they would obtain the amount they required, viz., £3,000,000, and they would then receive the remain- ing support necessary from the London financial houses. _

On Thursday evening a public meeting was held in the Eccles Town Hall. when it was resolved to form what was termed a Ship Canal Share Society. The society, according to the proposed rules, is to be conducted by a committee, to whom subscrip- tions will be paid. No subscriber will be able to buy less than one share or subscribe less than Is per week.
ItIINCORN.

Under the direction of Mr. J. W. Lightburn, local agent for the Manchester Ship Canal Company, a canvass has been started for the purpose of ascer- taining the extent of the support which the scheme is likely to meet with. Already a large number of shares have been taken up, and Runcorn people are hopefully looking forward to the success of the undertaking.
WARRINGTON.

The canvass in Warrington on behalf of the ship Canal is being actively prosecuted, and the canvas- sers, we understand, are meeting with much that is very encouraging, as shares are being. taken 'up. i freely, and there s a good prospect of raising the contributions from Warrington up to .£200,000. A meeting of the Executive Committee, appointed to manage the canvass of the town, was held on Thursday evening in the Council Chamber, at the Town Hall, when arrangements were made to can- vass the remaining polling districts. It may he mentioned that a circular is being issued by the committee calling attention to the advantages that the canal would confer upon Warrington if made. Th e committee, however, do not ask local investors to take shares because of these more or less direct ad- vantages, but because every member is thoroughly satisfied that the canal will prove a perfectly safe and remunerative investment. It is also pointed out that unless this district supports the scheme liber- ally and promptly the remainder of the capital may not be obtained in time.

- - - A Cabinet Council, which sat 2 hours and 20 minutes,: met at the Foreign Office on Friday. Tbe King of the Belgians and suite left Charing Cross Station by the 9-40 express on Friday morning en route for Ostend. A rock slide has occurred near Buenovista, Colorado, by which eight persons were killed, and several others injured. The Central News is authorised to state that Mr. William Evelyn, the Conservative member for Deptford, will not support the Irish Crimes Bill. The installation of Lord Egerton of Tattoo as Right Wor- shipful Provincial Grand Master of Cheshire took placelm Friday at Chester Town Hall. At the Good Tempters Grand Lodge of England in-Lon- don on Friday, resolutions were passed reiterating the pre- vious decision and confirming the order prohibiting kissing games. Mr. Chamberlain. who left Ayr, on Friday, was received In Edinburgh by deputations from the Edinburgh branch of the National Radical Union and the Liberal Unionist Association. The "Globe" says :—There is no foundation for the statement published that the Chancellor of the Exchequer intends to propose a grant of £200.000 to the funds of the Imperial Institute. MVIIDNIZ IN IRELAND.—Three men, named M`Gowan, Guildfoyle, and loran, have been arrested at Gort, near Loughrea, county Galway, on a charge of murdering a farmer named Baker, who has been missing since Christ- mas, and whose dead body was found a few days aga near his residence. Baker was the brother-in-law of M‘Gowan, and there had been a dispute respecting land. '
AMERICA AND THE CRIMES BILL
Nwtv Yons, FRIDAY.—Large meetings have been held at Brooklyn, Washington, and Baltimore to protest against the Irish Crimes Bill. THE ATTEMPT ON THE CZAR. _

VIENNA, FRIDAY.—he Tayblatt announces that the Czar was wounded in the arm in the attempt made upon la,a lite on the 29th ult. The Czarina is reported to be suffering from acute nervous disease. FATAL FIRE IN A HOTEL—FOUR LIVES - LOST.

Three dead bodies were afterwards found by ttre firemen under the debris.

FREEHOLDERS' MEWITHOg-A meeting of freeholders of the parish of Frodsham, was held In the Kingsley Chapel, at the Parish Church, oYertion, on Monday afternoon, when the Rev. H. B. div.head: WRECK OF A CHANNEL STEAMER. 20 PASSENGERS DROWNED-
div.p: THE WRECK OF A CHANNEL STEAMER. 20 PASSENGERS DROWNED-

DIEPPE, WEDNESDAY NIGNT.—The circumstances relating to the wreck of the Channel steamer Victoria on the rocks of Varengeville this morning' are as follows :—At ten minutes past four o'elock,.l when the steamer was close upon the coast,. &dense fog prevailed, and as the fog horn signal at the lighthouse was not sounding those on board had no, indication of the peril they were in. The fog horn, indeed, did not sound until some time after the vessel had struck. As the Victoria remained firmly fixed, the excitement increased, and, when, at 545,. Captain Clarke ordered the boats to be. lowered, many of the female passengers were in a state of abject panic. Unfortunately during the lower- ing of one of the boats a lady's cloak becamel entangled in one of the davits, with the result that the boat was almost immediately capsized, the whole of its occupants were thrown into the water, and the air was rent with the terrified shrieks of women and children. ,Every effort in roscuing them was made, but in spite of all that coule' be I done several were drowned. Three female bodies-1 and that of a child were washed ashore this evening, but no others have up to the time of telegraphing been recorded, and the entire number of lives lost is not yet known. Boats containing 37, passengers have reached Fecamp in safety, and another landed several more at Dieppe, where they now remain.. Captain Clarke stood by his vessel till 11 o'clock. He is one of the oldest and most experienceclofficers, in the service. The vessel is a total wreck. The prefect of the Department of the Seine Inferieure,, the Englieh Consul, and the Commissary of Marine, are giving all the assistance in their power to the survivors. The Dieppe lifeboat has been for a long; time engaged in picking up what luggage is still floating, but the greatest part of this is lost. The. names of the drowned have not yet been, ascer- tained. The Press Association's special correspondent at Newhaven telegraphs :-The loss of life is nowthought- to be more than was at first supp3sed. Several, bodies have been picked up by Captain White and landed at Dieppe, but owing to the fact that Chan- nel steamers do not take the names of passengers it is impossible yet to ascertain who is drowned. The carpenter is reported to be missing, but he is the. only member of the crew supposed tolpe lost. Cap- tain Clarke was injured in the hand while en- deavouring to restrain the passengers from over- crowding the boats. The " Times " Dieppe correspondent telegraphs later details of the disaster on the French coast. i The ladies got into the first boat, but some gentle- men jumped in also as it was being lowered. A lady's shawl fouled the block, and the boat cap- sized. Four only were saved. A second boat was filled,. but it was swamped and drifted to leeward. At the lowest computation 20 have perish et,, but their names are not yet obtainable. They- are, mostly of French nationality. Another amount says the loss.of lifaby the disas- ter to the cross-Channel steamer Victoria is now placed at about fourteen, a figure arrived at seem- ingly by comparing the issue of tickets with the number of passengers who have rendered an ac- count of themselves. -

A telegram received at Hanley on Thursday i morning, states that Mrs. Swift, of Hanley, and her two sons, were drowned in the wreck of the steam- ship Victoria. A telegram has also been received from one of the surviving children worded as fol- lows :—" Mother and two brothers drowned." Mrs., Swift was proceeding with her family to join her husband, who is employed at a china manufactory at Geneva. It is now believed that 20 lives were lost in the, disaster to the steamer Victoria, including three persons crushed to death between the port quarter. boat and the ship, and ;three children who are thought to have been drowned while asleep in the fore cabin. Two more bodies have been fund, these being of men. The Victoria, as last seen on Thursday evening, lies deep up the rocks, and she appears to be breaking up fast. LATEST DETAILS. A telegram received last night says the number of passengers now known to have been saved is 65, leaving from fifteen to twenty still unaccounted for, exclusive of those whose bodies have been re- covered. It is almost certain that four or five bodies will be found in the cabin of the steamer, and there is therefore little doubt that the total loss of life will amount to from 20 to 25. It is probable, however, that the exact number Win never be known, owing to the absence of passenger lists and the fact that many bodies must have been swept out to sea.

FALL OUT OF A RAILWAY °Amnion WnqDow. —A Golborne girl, named Smith, aged seven, bad a miraculous ekape OD the railway on Saturday morning when traveiling from Golborne to Wigan. As the train was passing Swinge grancia, where there is a complete network of railway lines, the carriage door opened, and the child fell forward on to the ground. When picked up her bead was injured, ark she was otherwise bruised and sb.kken. She was taken on to Wigan. The spot where the accident occurred is noted for heavy traffic, but fortunately this was a slack day, other. wise the child would in all probability have been caught by a passing train and killed.

THE COERCION BILL.

The adjourned debate oa Sir 13. Samuelson's amendment to the Motion for the second reading of the Criminal Law Amendment (Ireland) Bill was resumed.—Sir W. HennOurcrt opposed the Bill. He compared the present measure with, the bills introduced by former Governments, and pointed out that in none of them were provisions as stringent ale those in the meastire now under consideration. He con- tendvd that the sot-Tort of the Irish Nationalists was ob- tained by the' Tories on the ground that a Tory. Government would not introduce a Coercion Bill. He insisted that the real aim and object of the bill was to prevent legitimate combination on the part of the tenants of Ireland to protect themselves against oppressive land- ' lords.—Mr. PUMICE; on behalf of the Goverronttnt, said the Government had every hope that they would not be, obliged to d!spese with the services of Sir Redvers —Mr. RIIS9ELL opposed the bill and condemned that por- tion of it which affected the public press.—Mr. Crsr.:GE sup- ported the bill and justified its being made permanent.—Mr.. HARSINGTON denouaced the bill, more especially that part of it which gave summary jarisdiction to resident magistrates.

SAILING MATCH ON THE MERSEY.

OP Saturday, the 17th annual handicap sailing, match in connection with the -.Warringten, Sailing Club took place on the Mersey. the- race being from Runcorn to Warring- ton, The weather was beautifully fine, and,. although the time at which it was stated the- beam might be expected to be in sight was early ip the afternoon, between two and three thousand per.:. sons assembled, and lined the bank of the river, in. anticipation of witnessing the finish of the race. A considerable amount of money changed hands over the event, which, being an annual one, has become. well-known. The following boats were entered for competition, and all turned up ;—May Fly,,J, Davi- son, captain; Lily, J. Emery, captain; MischiefY E: Gleave, captain ; Primrose. 'S. Spencer, cap- Taal.; Deerfoot, T. Skelhorn, captain; Flor- ence, H. Warburton, captain; and. Gipsy, J.,. Leigh, captain. The whole, of the boats sported the, club flag, and made rather an imposing spectacle as they left Warrington en route for Runcorn prior, to,. the race. The starter had them under his control:at the appointed time, and sent them off to a goo&1 start. From the starting point up to Houghton Marsh point the race was very fairly contested, the boats continually passing and re-passing each other. It was at this point that Lily first came- to grief by not answering to her helm; and -at this. point also the scratch boat, Gipsy, began to over- haul her leaders. She passed Mischief and Deerfbot at the commencement of Fiddler's Ferry retch, and' went in hot pursuit, .of the remainder. When, ap- proaching the Ferry, the remaining four.. boats Came in close order. The race was a tight one rip to Poo-mouth brook, when Gipsy first came to 'the front: She • retained her position up to the,firhish of the race, winning by about 200 yards. . FlOrencel and Primrose made a dead-heat for second piece, Deerfoot Was fourth, Mayfly fifth, Mischief sixth, and Lily seventh. Owing to the ebb of the tide the boats failed to reach the winning post,which rather disappointed the spectators. The committee state that they endeavoured to make the raceas fair as possible for the whole of the boats, delaying the start as.lorig as they thought prudent to enable the boats first reaching the buoy to pass round without waiting for the ebb. Owing to a. swift running tide, and a head wind, it was cut rather too fine, hence'the result. In consequence, they have-decided to have another race as soon as one can be arranged. After the race the whole of the boats' clitws assem- bled at the Roe Buck Inn, Bridge-street,. and par- took of a substantial supper provided by Mr. J. Massey, the host. Business was transacted, and prizes presented, and the evening was .brcfrught to a close in a most enjoyable manner,

Doe AT LattGE.—At the Newton Petty Salmons, on Saturday„ befere Colonel McCorquodale, Meow R. Houghton, A. C. MeCorquodale, and W. F. Gooch, John Bryce, of Newton, was summoned for allowing his clog to be at large, Edward Walker appeared, and said the defendant, who was the manager of Mr Gillespie' paper works, was unable to attend.—P.C. Parker then stated that on Sunday fcronoon. 27th ultimo, he BM the defendant's sheep dog at large in Mill-lane, Newton. He wont to defendant's house, and the defendant's daughter said she did not know bow the dog had got out.—P.S. Comrnins gave corroborative evid- ence —The man Walker said the dog was being fed in the house, and when someone called at the' door the dog ran out. The defendant bad been at 'great trouble to see the dog was kept muzzled or fastened up since the byelaw came into force. The dog, however, was quite harmless, as It was almost blind and very old. Witness shot the dog ore the following Monday.—The Bench, on hearing this explains- ktion, dismissed the can on the paymeqt of the costs,

Mr W T Husbaad, the deputy coroner, on Ttiesdav even- ing held an-inquest at Widnes ,Police Court. 'touching the . death of Joseph Swift, 57 years of age, who had resided at 23, Deacon-road, Widnes. The deceased was employed as a fireman at the works of Messrs George Pilkington and Sons,, and should have worked from Saturday evening until te, o'clock on Sunday morning. John McMahon, the watch.. man, who resides at 7, Vine-street, deposed that he saw .the deceased in the works at seven o'clock, and be had no right to leave the yard.—Maria Casey, of Tanhouse-lanei stated that Swift came to her house at Di.30.0u Saturday ~ night and asked for a light for his pipe. Holed some blood on his cheek, and appeared to have been falling. Ao he walked away in the direction of Deacon-road he stag- gered.—William Cooper, a carter, said he found the deceased leaning against the wall in the middle of the goods yard on ethe Cheshire Lines Railway. lie was bleeding 'from one of his cheek bones, and said that he had fallen down. He had, he said,, been to Sally Price's for a drink, and he had a bottle-of whiskey in his pocket. He was not in a fit condition to go to work..-- Thomas Gillow, an engine driver,' of Lugsdale-road, said: that about eleven o'clock on Sunday moiming he found the deceased lying on the four-foot of the siding ,lead-- ing from Messrs Pilkington's Works to the Cheshire Linear No traffic had passed that way since Saturday afternoon, - and it appeared to witness that the man had fallen from the wall five feet high, which ran alongside. The only way. he, could get back to his work unnoticed, if he had left the yardy was by climbing over this wall.—P.C. Dowerbank, who had made an examination of the body, and had tracked the foot- prints of his shoes, slid he had not the alightest doubt :that- he had fallen over the wall, and time, met his death.-7-& verdict of accidental death was returned,

EASTER MONDAY. - The majorityr of the shopsinethe village were closed on Enster Monday the whole dayttand in the afternoon there was a considerable influx of visitors from the neighbouring towns, many driving over ancl,pat.- ting up at the various public.houses in the village. Lemsr PARISH Cnuncx,—The church of St. Maya,. Lymm, was, as is the general custom, delorated in honour of the Easter festival. The most prominent parts of the church were tastefully beautified, moss, daffodils, and prim-- roses being largely used. The pulpit was undertaken by Miss Battersby, the windows by Mrs. Peter Stubs, the - Misses Stubs, and Mrs Bower, and the font by Mrs Till.. Norris. VESTRY MEETING.—The vestry meetir.g of Lymm Par:sh Church was held on Tuesday evening, the rector, the G. W. Guest, presiding. Mr. Bayley wa&nominated by the chairman as rector's warden, and Mr. T. Jones was elected, parishioners' warden. As rector's sidesmen Mr. Adden. brook and Mr. T. A. Jones were appointed, and as parishioners' eidesmen Mr. Itohmar and Mr. H. Harrison.. Mr. T. Ardern and Mr. J. Smith were elected lay delegates.. The churchwardens' statement of accounts,sbowed a balance in hand of nearly £5. CHILDREN'S SALE OF WORK —A sale of work, consisting e of children's clothing, toys, dm., was hold in the infants school, Pepper•street, Lymm, on Monday. The stalls were tastefully arranged round dip room, and presided over by the Misses Davies, Miss Callender, Miss Owen, Mrs S. Lee, Mrs Fox, Miss Holt, and the refreshment stall by Miss Battersby and Mrs Ernest Crosfield. In the afternoon an,' entertainment was given by the infants, ccosisting of songs; dialognes,recitations, and dumb-bell exeraises, after which- & tea was provided for them. The bazaar was visited by a , large number of persons in the course of the afternoon and evening, the amount realised being about LSO.: which will be devoted to defraying the expenses of the Children's', Scripture Union.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF ,GIJARMANS,:
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF ,GIJARMANS,:

The fortnightly meeting of the Present Board 0 Guar- 1 diens was held at the:Union Workhouse, Wbiston, on Thurs- day forenoon, when there were present Mr J Lowe (chair- man), the Rev Dean Finegan, Messrs James Fisher, E Syder. Jamea Birchall, W Middleburst, J: Jackson, J Buck- ley, C B Johnson, W Tyner, J Whalley, .1 Griffiths, J Leatherbarrow, J idsnwright, WB Longton, R A Graves, and S II Hartley (clerk). RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 481 inmates of the house this week, against 492 Met week, and 482 in the corresponding week last year ;• 62 vagrants bacli been relieved, againt 51 last year. Crirrs TO Ilia WORM-101SM —The Workhouse Muter reported that the Rev. Thomas Chambers and Mr. William Middlehurst (members Of the Board) had sent a supply of flowers for the Workhouse inmates, and the thanks of the Board were tendered tathose gentlemen for their gifts. It was stated that Mr. Middlehurst had from time to Arne sent a quantity of plants which were admirably sui%tble for the sick, ward. PAYMEZUS TO ARLEY PENSIVNEES.—A circular letter was read from. the Woolwich Guardians asking the Board to support aepetitien to the Local Government Board in favour of the payments of pensions to army men, drc., weekly or monthly instead of quarterly as at present. It waa stated that considerable inconvenience and trouble arose through the long payment system, and the Board decided to support the petition. Ths " INDEFITIGABL4" MYSTEJILY.—The Clerk briefly referred to the mysterious disappearance of lolen Ellison, thirteen years of age, from the training ship Indefatigable, and' said the boy had been chargeable to the Prescot Union, but the Guardians cemented to his being put apprentice to tha master of the vesael. Ile produced the indentures, dated l'itivember fe'e 1885. Mrs Ellison. the boy's mother, who lived in Irwell-street, Widnes, had been to him in great dis- tress, but he had been obliged to tell the poor woman that the Guardians wore unable to do anything. The clerk added that "If anything should arise to en ible me to help the poor mother I suppose I have your authority to do what I can ?" Several Guardians exclaimed "Certainly !" and the clerk was instructed to render any assistance he could under the sad cimumatances. Tim EIKE4I2I.TION OP Curmertres.--Thee Clerk read several cemmunications with reference to the whereabouts of the children sent out by the Boaed to Canada some time ago. It appeared that the Local Government Board had ob- taMed information relative to some of the childten, but there were several others of whom they bad not been able to gain information,—The Rev. Dean Finegan said they had sent information to the Local Goverunaent Board by which the other children could be traced. VOTES or THemKs.—This being the last meeting of the Beard's year, the Rey. Doan Finegan moved a vote of thanks to the chairman for his servioenduring the year. He arid the chairman bad discharged his duties not only effici- ently but with courtesy to every member of the Board.— The motion was carried, and, in responding, the Chairman said his duties had been rendered lighter by the kind assist- ance he had received from all the members. He returned his thanks for their kindness and courtesy.—On the motion of Mr. Tyrer, a similar compliment was paid to Messes, James Fisher and William Bluebell, the. vige-ch4irtgeu, This wa4 the princiPul business.

The ANNUAL DISTRICT MEETING of the Members of the above Society, resident in WARRINGTON and DISTRICT, will be held within the BRITISH WORKMAN, TIORSEMARKET-STREET. on the evening of TR lIRSDAF, 28TH Arum, 1887, at Eight o'clock. BUSINESS : To appoint a Chairman and Secretary, and to elect Delegates to represent the District at the meetings of the Society, all in terms of Rule's. Members 21 years of age and upwards, and who have been 26 weeks in the SecietY, admitted to the meeting on showing their Contribution Books. Only those Members residing in the District who are 25 yeare of age or upwards, two years in Membership and in full benefit, are eligible to be elected as Delegates. By order of the Board of Management. DAVID FORTUNE, President. WILLIAM THOM, Treasurer. WIT. W. NOT BY EDGAR ALLAN POE? Once upon a midnight 'dreary, in bed quite weak and weary, With sleeplessness, lone spirits, and Indigestion sore; While I strove in vain at napping, suddenly there came a tapping, As of some one gently rapping—nipping at my Chamber door "It's Doctor Draughts," I muttered, "tapping at my cham- ber door. 'Twas the Doctor, nothing more. Oh I distinctly I remember; it was in the bleak December, And in every single member of my body pains I bore Eagerly I whaled the morrow, vainly had I sought to borrow Frdin drugs surcease of sorrow--sorrow for my pains galore; And Leaked if I should ever be as healthy as before; Quoth the Doctor—. Nevermore! "Your chest is bad, that's certain; your neuralgia's always hurtle, g, And your liver is so sluggish that life's to you is bore; And your heart's so bad at beating that In vain you're sleep entreating, While from weakness eves now you perspire from every pore"— ' But.
